sources.name: Open-Meteo Forecast API (precipitation forecast)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: access-control-allow-headers: accept, authorization, content-type, origin, x-requested-with, user-agent, access-control-allow-origin | access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS | access-control-max-age: 600
sources.preflightResult: OPTIONS with Origin+Access-Control-Request-Method returned HTTP/1.1 200 OK, Content-Length: 0, and the identical three CORS headers. Preflight fully supported.
sources.format: JSON (default); CSV via &format=csv; XLSX/FlatBuffers also offered
sources.contentEncoding: gzip served only when the client sends Accept-Encoding: gzip (observed 'Content-Encoding: gzip'). Default curl request without that header returned chunked, uncompressed. Browsers always send it, so gzip is automatic in-app.
sources.rateLimit: NO rate-limit headers of any kind observed (grepped for ratelimit/x-/retry/quota on a 200 GET - none present). 20 rapid sequential GETs all returned 200 with no throttling. Documented free non-commercial limit is ~10k calls/day but this is NOT observable from headers, so the app cannot self-monitor quota.
sources.coverage: Global. Probed 38.95,-77.12 (US) and 27.7,85.3 (Nepal) - both fine. Grid snap at Nepal was 27.732864,85.24719 (~9 km ECMWF IFS grid).
sources.enables: 16-day precipitation outlook (daily sum, wet-hours count, and probability-of-precip) at any site, driving a near-term inflow/generation forecast panel.
sources.freeFields: elevation: 1288.0 (metres, model grid cell elevation - free DEM value on every weather call); timezone: "Asia/Kathmandu"; timezone_abbreviation: "GMT+5:45"; utc_offset_seconds: 20700; latitude/longitude echoed as the SNAPPED grid centre (27.732864, 85.24719) which reveals model resolution; generationtime_ms: 0.143; daily_units: {precipitation_sum: "mm", precipitation_hours: "h", precipitation_probability_max: "%"}
sources.gotchas: MAX forecast_days = 16; forecast_days=17 errors with the off-by-one message {"error":true,"reason":"Forecast days is invalid. Allowed range 0 to 16. Given 16."} (it echoes 16, not 17 - do not trust the echoed number when debugging). Multi-location comma-separated lat/lon returns HTTP 200 and a JSON ARRAY instead of an object - parser must branch on Array.isArray. timezone=auto is needed or you get GMT day boundaries, which mis-bins monsoon daily totals by ~6h in Nepal.

sources.name: Open-Meteo Historical Archive API (ERA5 reanalysis)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: access-control-allow-headers: accept, authorization, content-type, origin, x-requested-with, user-agent, access-control-allow-origin | access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS | access-control-max-age: 600
sources.preflightResult: Not separately required for simple GET; same CORS header set present on the 200 GET. Host shares the identical CORS config as api.open-meteo.com.
sources.contentEncoding: gzip (measured). 35-year daily precipitation_sum = 231,679 bytes raw vs 39,283 bytes gzipped (5.9x). Full 86-year 1940-2025 series = 573,995 raw / 105,626 gzipped. Three sites x 30 years in one multi-location call = 110,600 gzipped.
sources.rateLimit: No rate-limit headers observed. Heavy multi-decade queries returned in normal time; generationtime_ms up to ~84 ms for a 1940 single-day query.
sources.coverage: Global, 1940-01-01 to 2026-08-11 (present). Confirmed by error: {"error":true,"reason":"Parameter 'start_date' is out of allowed range from 1940-01-01 to 2026-08-11"}. 1930 rejected, 1940 works. Coverage is genuinely poor in complex terrain: ERA5's 0.25 deg cell cannot represent a Himalayan valley - see gotchas.
sources.enables: Multi-decade daily precipitation climatology at any site: monsoon-vs-dry-season ratio, wet/dry year ranking, and a first-order rainfall-runoff inflow estimate where no gauge exists.
sources.freeFields: elevation: 1288.0 (m, grid-cell elevation); latitude/longitude echoed as the SNAPPED grid centre - this is the single best free diagnostic of which model you actually got (era5 -> 27.75,85.25 exactly on the 0.25 deg grid; best_match/ecmwf_ifs -> 27.732864,85.24719 on the ~9 km IFS grid); daily_units.precipitation_sum: "mm"; generationtime_ms; timezone/utc_offset_seconds. Computed live from one call: Kathmandu ERA5 1991-2020 monthly means Jan 44.1, Jul 777.9, Dec 19.7 mm; JJAS 2211 mm vs DJFM 168 mm = 13.2x monsoon:dry ratio.
sources.gotchas: UNITS: precipitation_sum is mm (confirmed in daily_units). (1) THE BIG ONE - the default models=best_match is NOT a homogeneous series. It equals ERA5 exactly through 2016 (0 of 92 JJA days differ in 2010/2014/2016) then silently switches to a higher-resolution model on ~2017-01-01 (91-92 of 92 JJA days differ in 2017/2020/2024; JJA 2020 total best_match 2809.1 mm vs era5 2426.0 mm, a 16% step). Any trend or normals calculation on the default series is contaminated by a model discontinuity at 2017. MUST pass &models=era5 explicitly for multi-decade work. (2) models=era5_land returns ALL NULLS for precipitation_sum - verified at Nepal (2020/2023/2024/2025 all [None]) and at Potomac US (snap 39.0,-77.1 -> [None,None,None]). ERA5-Land precipitation is a dead end here; do not offer it as the 'higher resolution' option. (3) Resolution/bias: same day 2024-07-01 Kathmandu gives era5 9.5 mm vs ecmwf_ifs 34.8 mm - a 3.7x disagreement. And ERA5 1991-2020 annual total at Kathmandu comes out 2765 mm vs a real-world station value near 1400-1600 mm, i.e. roughly 2x too wet in this valley. ERA5 precipitation in mountainous terrain must be bias-corrected before it is used for any energy-yield number.

sources.name: Open-Meteo Elevation API (batch elevation profile)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: access-control-allow-headers: accept, authorization, content-type, origin, x-requested-with, user-agent, access-control-allow-origin | access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS | access-control-max-age: 600
sources.preflightResult: Same CORS header set observed on the 200 GET; Content-Length: 35 for the 3-point query. POST also returns 200, so POST is a legitimate transport.
sources.format: JSON, minimal: {"elevation":[81.0, 1288.0, 418.0]} - metres, array order matches input order, coordinates NOT echoed
sources.contentEncoding: Not compressed at this size (Content-Length: 35 for 3 points, plain). 100-point response measured at 659 bytes - too small for gzip to matter.
sources.rateLimit: No rate-limit headers observed. Ran escalating batches (10/100/101/110/120/150/199/200/300/500/1000) back to back with no throttling.
sources.coverage: Global including bathymetry-as-zero. Sanity check: Everest 27.9881,86.9250 -> 8724.0 m (real 8849 - a ~125 m low bias typical of a 90 m DEM at a sharp summit); Dead Sea 31.5,35.5 -> -427.0 m (real ~-430, correct and negative values ARE supported); open ocean 0.0,-30.0 -> 0.0 m.
sources.enables: Client-side long-profile / head calculation: sample the penstock or river centreline and get the gross head and slope without any server, in 100-point chunks.
sources.freeFields: Only the elevation array is returned - no station metadata, no coordinates echoed. Compensating free fields: EVERY other Open-Meteo endpoint (forecast, archive, flood) returns 'elevation' for its own grid cell anyway, so a single flood/forecast call already gives you a free (coarse) elevation without touching this endpoint.
sources.gotchas: HARD LIMIT = 100 COORDINATES PER REQUEST. Exact error at 101+: {"error":true,"reason":"Parameter 'latitude' and 'longitude' must not exceed 100 coordinates."} POST DOES NOT BYPASS IT - 150 coords via POST body returned the same 400 error. Escalation results: N=10 200, N=100 200, N=101 400, N=200 400, N=300 400, N=500 414, N=1000 414 (the 414 URI-Too-Long masks the real API error at large N, so a naive tester would misdiagnose it as a URL-length problem). A 100-coordinate GET URL is 1458 chars - comfortably under browser/CDN limits, so GET chunking is fine and POST buys nothing. DEM is ~90 m (Copernicus GLO-90): elevation changes across 0.001 deg steps (85.300 -> 1288.0, 85.301 -> 1290.0, 85.302 -> 1287.0), so sampling finer than ~0.001 deg returns interpolation noise, not real terrain. For a 1000-point profile budget 10 sequential requests.

sources.name: Open-Meteo Flood API (GloFAS river discharge)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: access-control-allow-headers: accept, authorization, content-type, origin, x-requested-with, user-agent, access-control-allow-origin | access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS | access-control-max-age: 600
sources.preflightResult: Same three CORS headers present on the 200 GET; separate hostname (flood-api.open-meteo.com) but identical CORS config to api.open-meteo.com.
sources.contentEncoding: gzip. Full 1997-01-01..2026-08-10 daily series: JSON 209,745 raw / 45,944 gzipped; CSV 187,994 raw / 54,705 gzipped. JSON+gzip is the smallest option - CSV is smaller raw but compresses WORSE, so do not switch to CSV to save bandwidth.
sources.rateLimit: No rate-limit headers observed. Ran a 16-cell grid scan (16 sequential calls) plus dozens of date probes with no throttling or 429.
sources.coverage: Global GloFAS v4 at 0.05 deg. Data 1997-01-01 to present + ~206 days ahead. Coverage is genuinely poor for ANY small catchment - the limitation is resolution, not geography, and it bites equally in the US, Nepal and Switzerland.
sources.enables: Free 29-year daily discharge history plus a ~7-month-ahead ensemble outlook at any point on a mapped river - a flow-duration curve and seasonal generation forecast with no gauge and no backend.
sources.freeFields: daily_units.river_discharge: "m³/s" (CUBIC METRES per second - metric, unlike USGS which is cubic feet per second; no conversion needed for SI but you MUST convert if mixing with USGS); elevation: 569.0 (m, free cell elevation); latitude/longitude echoed as the snapped GloFAS cell centre (27.925003, 85.125) - essential for showing the user which cell they actually got; generationtime_ms; timezone. ENSEMBLE SPREAD IS FREE: daily=river_discharge_mean,river_discharge_median,river_discharge_max,river_discharge_min,river_discharge_p25,river_discharge_p75 all return in one call (e.g. Trishuli 2026-08-11 mean 628.22, median 628.51, min 614.18, max 647.63, p25 622.38, p75 632.87) - that is a free uncertainty band. &ensemble=true additionally exposes river_discharge_member01..NN individual members.
sources.gotchas: UNITS CONFIRMED FROM LIVE RESPONSE: m³/s. (1) DATE-RANGE LIE: the API ACCEPTS start_date back to 1984-01-01 (error text says 'allowed range from 1984-01-01 to 2027-08-11') but every value from 1984-01-01 to 1996-12-31 is NULL. Real data starts 1997-01-01. Requesting from 1984 returns 15,563 points of which only 10,814 are non-null - you pay 4,749 null days (~28% wasted payload, 290,941 vs 209,745 bytes) for nothing. Always request start_date=1997-01-01. Once past 1997 there are ZERO interior gaps. (2) GRID RESOLUTION IS 0.05 deg (~5.5 km), measured directly: sweeping longitude in 0.01 deg steps, cell centres snapped to -77.12499 then -77.174995 - exactly 0.05 apart. (3) SMALL RIVERS ARE NOT RESOLVED - BLUNTLY. Two adjacent cells 2.8 km apart on the Potomac returned 1.61 m³/s and 140.91 m³/s. A 4x4 cell scan around Zurich returned: 50.64, 0.36, 0.52, 0.34 / 0.08, 0.83, 0.61, 0.03 / 0.89, 0.03, 0.02, 0.0 / 0.95, 1.23, 1.20, 1.19. Exactly one cell carries the river; every neighbour returns a near-zero local-runoff number that LOOKS like a plausible small-stream flow and is meaningless. The Limmat at Zurich (real ~90 m³/s) returned 0.95 m³/s because the snap missed the channel. A run-of-river scheme on a catchment below roughly 500-1000 km² CANNOT be sized from this API - the user will silently get either a hillslope cell (~0-1 m³/s) or the wrong, much larger trunk river. (4) Where it DOES land on the network it is well calibrated: Potomac mainstem cell 1997-2026 min 30.77 / median 202.0 / max 5545.26 m³/s against a real Little Falls median near 190 m³/s; Trishuli 622.73 m³/s and Bagmati at Kathmandu 27.18 m³/s in August are both plausible monsoon values. (5) Forecast horizon is ~206 non-null days (requested 210, got 206 non-null, last 2027-03-04); forecast_days accepts 300 and 366 with HTTP 200 but the extra days are null. (6) Multi-location comma syntax returns a JSON ARRAY.

sources.name: Open-Meteo Seasonal Forecast API (monsoon-scale outlook)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: access-control-allow-headers: accept, authorization, content-type, origin, x-requested-with, user-agent, access-control-allow-origin | access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS | access-control-max-age: 600
sources.preflightResult: Same CORS header set observed on the 200 GET. Distinct hostname seasonal-api.open-meteo.com, same permissive config.
sources.contentEncoding: Chunked; gzip available with Accept-Encoding. Default response is large because all 50 members are returned whether you want them or not (~62 KB for one variable).
sources.rateLimit: No rate-limit headers observed.
sources.coverage: Global. Returned 183 days from 2026-08-11 to 2027-02-09 - i.e. a full monsoon-into-dry-season transition in one call.
sources.enables: Six-month-ahead ensemble precipitation outlook, giving a probabilistic monsoon-strength signal for the coming season rather than a single deterministic line.
sources.freeFields: 50 ENSEMBLE MEMBERS FREE: daily_units contains precipitation_sum_member01 .. precipitation_sum_member50, all in "mm", alongside the deterministic precipitation_sum. That is a ready-made probability fan (p10/p50/p90) computable client-side with no extra requests. Also elevation: 1288.0, timezone, generationtime_ms, and the snapped lat/lon 27.681498,85.22124.
sources.gotchas: Separate hostname - seasonal-api.open-meteo.com, NOT api.open-meteo.com; a wrong host silently 404s. Default lead time is 183 days; forecast_days=180 correctly returns 180. The 50 members are returned by default and dominate payload - there is no way observed to suppress them, so budget ~62 KB per variable. Seasonal skill for precipitation in the Himalaya is weak in absolute terms; use the ensemble SPREAD as the message, not the ensemble mean as a prediction.

sources.name: Open-Meteo Climate API (CMIP6 downscaled projections)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: access-control-allow-headers: accept, authorization, content-type, origin, x-requested-with, user-agent, access-control-allow-origin | access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS | access-control-max-age: 600
sources.preflightResult: Same CORS header set observed on the 200 GET. Distinct hostname climate-api.open-meteo.com.
sources.contentEncoding: Chunked; gzip on request. Not separately measured for a full multi-decade projection.
sources.rateLimit: No rate-limit headers observed. generationtime_ms 144 ms for a 3-model 3-day query - notably slower than the other endpoints, so multi-decade multi-model queries will be sluggish.
sources.coverage: Global, downscaled to ~10 km. Historical and future dates both served (2020 and 2050 both returned 200 with real values).
sources.enables: Long-horizon change signal: how the monsoon/dry-season precipitation split at a site shifts under CMIP6 scenarios, framing the multi-decade resource risk for a scheme.
sources.freeFields: Per-model variable naming is automatic and free: daily_units contains precipitation_sum_EC_Earth3P_HR, precipitation_sum_MPI_ESM1_2_XR, precipitation_sum_NICAM16_8S - one call yields a multi-model spread keyed by model name. Also elevation: 1288.0 and the snapped lat/lon 27.700005,85.30002 (~10 km downscaled grid, finer than raw ERA5).
sources.gotchas: NOT every listed model returns data for every period: EC_Earth3P_HR returned [null,null,null] for 2050-01-01..03 at Kathmandu while MPI_ESM1_2_XR and NICAM16_8S returned real values in the SAME response. Silent per-model nulls - the app must null-check each model series independently or a chart will show a phantom flat line. Separate hostname climate-api.open-meteo.com. Slowest endpoint in the cluster (144 ms generation for a trivial query).

notes:
VERDICT: the entire Open-Meteo cluster is browser-usable with no key, no proxy, no backend. Every one of the six hosts probed (api, archive-api, flood-api, seasonal-api, climate-api) returned the byte-identical CORS triple on a real GET, and a real OPTIONS preflight on api.open-meteo.com returned 200 with the same headers plus access-control-max-age: 600. Nothing in this cluster is a CORS dead end.

THE THREE FINDINGS THAT ACTUALLY CHANGE THE PRODUCT:

1. ELEVATION BATCH LIMIT IS EXACTLY 100 (the elevation-profile decision). Verified by escalation and bisection: N=100 -> 200, N=101 -> 400 with {"error":true,"reason":"Parameter 'latitude' and 'longitude' must not exceed 100 coordinates."}. POST does NOT raise it - 150 coords in a POST body returns the identical error. Note the trap: at N>=500 the request dies with HTTP 414 (URI too long) BEFORE reaching the API, which would lead a careless tester to blame URL length and try POST, which also fails. A 100-point GET URL is only 1458 chars, so GET chunking is correct and POST is pointless. Build the profile feature as ceil(points/100) sequential GETs; a 1000-point penstock profile is 10 requests and ~6.6 KB total. DEM is ~90 m Copernicus GLO-90 (values change across 0.001 deg steps), so sampling finer than ~0.001 deg is noise.

2. GLOFAS CANNOT SIZE A SMALL RUN-OF-RIVER SCHEME - be blunt about this in the UI. Measured grid is 0.05 deg (~5.5 km): sweeping longitude in 0.01 deg steps, cell centres snapped to -77.12499 then -77.174995, exactly 0.05 apart. The consequence is brutal and I measured it two ways. (a) Two adjacent Potomac cells 2.8 km apart: 1.61 vs 140.91 m³/s - an 88x jump. (b) A 4x4 cell scan around Zurich: 50.64 next to 0.36, 0.08, 0.03, 0.02, 0.0. Only cells ON the GloFAS river network carry flow; every neighbour returns a near-zero local-runoff value that looks like a believable small-stream discharge and is meaningless. The Limmat at Zurich (real ~90 m³/s) returned 0.95 m³/s because the snap missed the channel. Any catchment below roughly 500-1000 km² is unresolvable. The app MUST (i) display the returned snapped lat/lon and the distance from the user's click, (ii) let the user nudge to an adjacent cell, and (iii) refuse to quote a capacity number when the returned discharge is implausibly small for the drainage area. Where it DOES hit the network it is genuinely good: Potomac mainstem 1997-2026 median 202.0 m³/s vs a real Little Falls median near 190; Trishuli 622.73 and Bagmati Kathmandu 27.18 m³/s in August are both plausible monsoon values. Units confirmed live as m³/s (cubic METRES) - the opposite convention from USGS cubic feet per second, so any mixed USGS/GloFAS chart needs a 0.0283168 factor.

3. TWO SILENT DATA-RANGE / HOMOGENEITY TRAPS THE DOCS DO NOT WARN ABOUT.
   (a) Flood API: the error text advertises "allowed range from 1984-01-01 to 2027-08-11" and requests from 1984 return HTTP 200 - but every value before 1997-01-01 is NULL. Real record is 1997-01-01 onward: 10,814 non-null of 15,563 requested, with ZERO interior gaps. Requesting from 1984 wastes 4,749 null days (290,941 vs 209,745 bytes, ~28%). Hardcode start_date=1997-01-01.
   (b) Archive API: the default models=best_match is NOT a homogeneous series. It equals ERA5 exactly through 2016 (0 of 92 JJA days differ in 2010, 2014 and 2016) and then silently switches to a higher-resolution model at ~2017-01-01 (91-92 of 92 JJA days differ in 2017, 2020, 2024; JJA 2020 total 2809.1 mm best_match vs 2426.0 mm era5, a 16% step). Computing a monsoon-vs-dry ratio or any trend on the default series bakes in a fake 2017 discontinuity. Pass &models=era5 explicitly for anything multi-decade.

CORRECTION TO COMMON DOCS ASSUMPTIONS:
- models=era5_land is USELESS for precipitation here: precipitation_sum returned all nulls at BOTH test sites (Nepal 2020/2023/2024/2025 all [None]; Potomac snap 39.0,-77.1 -> [None,None,None]). Do not offer it as the "higher-resolution historical" option.
- Forecast API max is 16 days, and the 17-day rejection message is off by one - it says "Allowed range 0 to 16. Given 16." when you passed 17. Do not trust the echoed value when debugging.
- Flood API forecast_days accepts 300 and 366 with HTTP 200 but only ~206 days are non-null (last real day 2027-03-04). That ~7-month seasonal discharge outlook is the single most valuable free feature in this cluster for a hydropower app.

FREE FEATURES WORTH EXPLOITING (all ride along on calls you already make):
- elevation (metres) is returned by EVERY endpoint - forecast, archive, flood, seasonal, climate - so a coarse site elevation costs zero extra requests.
- The echoed latitude/longitude is always the SNAPPED grid centre, which both reveals the model resolution and is the honest thing to show the user ("you clicked X, we sampled Y, 2.4 km away").
- Flood ensemble statistics are free in one call: river_discharge_mean/median/max/min/p25/p75 (Trishuli 2026-08-11: mean 628.22, median 628.51, min 614.18, max 647.63, p25 622.38, p75 632.87). &ensemble=true adds individual members.
- Seasonal API returns 50 named ensemble members (precipitation_sum_member01..50) by default - a ready-made probability fan.
- Climate API auto-suffixes variables per model (precipitation_sum_MPI_ESM1_2_XR etc.) for a free multi-model spread.
- One archive call yields a full climatology: Kathmandu ERA5 1991-2020 gave monthly means (Jan 44.1 ... Jul 777.9 ... Dec 19.7 mm), JJAS 2211 mm vs DJFM 168 mm = 13.2x monsoon:dry ratio, annual 2765 mm, for 39 KB gzipped.

BIAS WARNING FOR ANY ENERGY-YIELD NUMBER: ERA5 precipitation in mountain terrain is badly biased locally. Same day 2024-07-01 at Kathmandu: era5 9.5 mm vs ecmwf_ifs 34.8 mm (3.7x disagreement). And the ERA5 1991-2020 annual total above (2765 mm) is roughly double the real-world station value near 1400-1600 mm for Kathmandu. The monsoon:dry RATIO is probably usable as a shape; the ABSOLUTE mm totals are not, and must be bias-corrected against a local gauge before any capacity or yield figure is shown.

PAYLOAD / BANDWIDTH SUMMARY (all measured): 35-yr daily precip 231,679 raw / 39,283 gzip; 86-yr (1940-2025) 573,995 / 105,626; 3 sites x 30 yr in one multi-location call 110,600 gzip; 29-yr flood history 209,745 / 45,944 gzip; 16-day forecast with hourly 10,155; 100-point elevation 659. Everything is comfortably in range for a static browser app. Note gzip is only served when Accept-Encoding is sent - automatic in browsers, but invisible to a naive curl test. CSV is smaller RAW but compresses WORSE than JSON (flood 29-yr: CSV 54,705 gzip vs JSON 45,944 gzip), so do not switch to CSV for bandwidth.

RATE LIMITS: no rate-limit headers of any kind exist on these responses (grepped for ratelimit/x-/retry/quota - none). 20 rapid sequential calls all 200; a 16-call grid scan plus dozens of date probes never throttled. The documented free non-commercial allowance (~10k/day) is therefore NOT self-monitorable from the client - the app should throttle and cache defensively rather than react to headers. HTTPS works on every host; plain http:// also returns 200 without redirect, but is irrelevant since mixed-content rules force HTTPS in a browser anyway.

Multi-location comma-separated lat/lon works on forecast, archive and flood (all HTTP 200) but returns a JSON ARRAY rather than an object - the client parser must branch on Array.isArray or it will break the moment someone compares two sites.

sources.name: World Bank Indicators API (hydro share of electricity)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: Access-Control-Allow-Headers: X-Requested-With ; Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET
sources.format: JSON (also XML, ?format=jsonstat). Response is a 2-element array: [meta, [observations]]
sources.preflightResult: OPTIONS with Origin + Access-Control-Request-Method: GET returned HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found with NO CORS headers. Simple GETs still work because they are not preflighted. CRITICAL: do NOT add any custom request header (e.g. X-Requested-With, Authorization, or a non-simple Content-Type) or the browser will preflight and the 404 will kill the request.
sources.contentEncoding: Content-Encoding: gzip when Accept-Encoding: gzip is sent
sources.rateLimit: No RateLimit-* / Retry-After headers observed. Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 (24h CDN cache via Cloudflare, CF-Cache-Status seen). No documented hard limit hit during probing.
sources.freeFields: indicator.id ('EG.ELC.HYRO.ZS'), indicator.value ('Electricity production from hydroelectric sources (% of total)'), country.id ('NP'), country.value ('Nepal'), countryiso3code ('NPL'), date ('2023'), value (99.0928407976463), unit (''), obs_status (''), decimal (1); meta block carries lastupdated ('2026-07-13'), page/pages/per_page/total. Query params mrnev=1 (most recent non-empty value) and per_page keep payloads tiny.
sources.gotchas: UNIT IS PERCENT, not energy. Value is % of total electricity production, and the API's own unit field is an EMPTY STRING. MAJOR CORRECTION: every absolute-energy indicator is listed in /v2/indicator but returns an error on data query - EG.ELC.HYRO.KH, EG.ELC.PROD.KH and EN.PRD.ELEC all return [{"message":[{"id":"175","key":"Invalid format","value":"The indicator was not found. It may have been deleted or archived."}]}]. Only the .ZS (% of total) series still serve data, so you CANNOT get hydro GWh from the World Bank any more. Error responses return HTTP 200 with an error object in the body, so check for the message key, not the status code.
sources.enables: A one-line national framing next to the user's result - 'Nepal generates 99.1% of its electricity from hydro' - fetched live in a 331-byte request with no key and no build step.
sources.coverage: Excellent and current worldwide: WLD returned 2024=16.12%, 2023=14.54%, 2022=15.25%, 2021=15.41%, 2020=16.56% (35 non-null of 66 obs). NPL 2023=99.09%, 2015=99.48%; USA present. Coverage is by country, so no sub-national or per-plant detail; small island states and conflict states have sparser series. Weakness is temporal density in the 1960s-70s and the total absence of absolute-energy series, not geography.

sources.name: Our World in Data - grapher CSV endpoint (single indicator)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: access-control-allow-methods: GET,OPTIONS,HEAD (on the OPTIONS preflight)
sources.preflightResult: OPTIONS with Origin + Access-Control-Request-Method: GET returned HTTP/1.1 204 No Content WITH Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and access-control-allow-methods: GET,OPTIONS,HEAD. Preflight passes cleanly - unlike the World Bank.
sources.contentEncoding: Not advertised on the plain GET (Content-Length: 233887 served identity); CSV compresses very well over the wire if the client sends Accept-Encoding
sources.rateLimit: None observed. Cloudflare-fronted, cf-cache-status present.
sources.freeFields: Entity ('ASEAN (Ember)', country names), Code (ISO3, blank for aggregates), Year (2000), Hydropower (50.43 - TWh of hydro generation). Includes regional aggregates and 'World' for free, which is exactly what a '% of country X's hydro' comparison needs.
sources.gotchas: SERVER-SIDE FILTERING DOES NOT WORK. Adding ?country=USA~NPL~CHE returned the identical 233887 bytes - the country param is a grapher UI selection, not a data filter. You always download the full ~234 KB and filter client-side. UNITS ARE TWh, not GWh, and the column header is literally 'Hydropower'. OWID varies units between grapher slugs, so re-confirm per indicator. The documented slug 301-redirects; a browser fetch follows it transparently.
sources.enables: The absolute-energy half of the comparison the World Bank can no longer provide: 'your scheme's 137 GWh/yr is 0.3% of Nepal's total hydro generation', computed from one keyless 234 KB fetch.
sources.coverage: Global by country plus regional aggregates and World, annual from 2000. Because it is Ember+EI-derived it is strong for all sizeable grids including Nepal, Switzerland and the US. notes:
## PART 1 — RUN-OF-RIVER BENCHMARK PLANTS (the priority deliverable)

Four real, published plants with citable numbers. I ran `P = rho*g*Q*H` against each to show what efficiency the published figures imply — this is the actual validation harness for the app's physics. rho=1000 kg/m3, g=9.81 m/s2. All arithmetic below was computed, not estimated.

### BENCHMARK 1 — Chilime, Nepal (HIGH HEAD, Pelton) — BEST QUALITY, single primary source
- Installed capacity: **22.1 MW** (2 x 11.05 MW; turbine nameplate quoted separately as 2 x 11.28 MW)
- Gross head: **351.5 m**; Net head: **337.46 m**
- Design discharge: **7.5 m3/s**
- Annual energy: **137.9 GWh** average ("137 million units"); deemed energy **132.9 GWh**
- Type: "Run of river with peaking pondages"; 2 x horizontal Pelton, digital governor; COD 2003-08-24
- SOURCE: plant operator's own site, Chilime Hydropower Company Ltd — https://www.chilime.com.np/en/plant/
- **Physics check: rho*g*Q*H_net = 24.83 MW -> implied eta = 0.890.** (Using gross head 351.5 m -> 25.86 MW -> eta = 0.855.)
- **Capacity factor = 137.9e3 MWh / (22.1 MW * 8760 h) = 0.712**
- WHY THIS IS THE BEST TEST CASE: capacity, gross head, net head, design flow and annual energy all come from one page, so there is no cross-source stitching. eta = 0.890 on net head is textbook for Pelton + generator. If your model reproduces 22.1 MW from (7.5 m3/s, 337.46 m, eta 0.89) it is correct.

### BENCHMARK 2 — Rheinfelden (new plant), Germany/Switzerland, High Rhine (LOW HEAD, Kaplan bulb)
- Installed capacity: **100 MW** (4 x 25 MW Kaplan bulb turbines)
- Average head: **8.5 m**
- Design discharge: **1500 m3/s**
- Annual average generation: **600 GWh**
- Recommissioned September 2011 (replaced the 1898 plant)
- SOURCE: Fichtner, the design engineer — https://www.fichtner.de/en/projects/detailpage/construction-of-rheinfelden-run-of-river-hydropower-plant-germany
- **Physics check: rho*g*Q*H = 1000*9.81*1500*8.5 = 125.08 MW -> implied eta = 0.800**
- **Capacity factor = 600e3 / (100 * 8760) = 0.685**
- **IMPORTANT CAVEAT — do not read eta=0.80 as the real turbine efficiency.** Fichtner publishes "average head", not rated head. A modern Kaplan bulb runs at eta ~0.90-0.92. At eta=0.90 and H=8.5 m, 1500 m3/s would yield 112.6 MW — more than the 100 MW nameplate, i.e. the units are generator-limited and the plant does not simultaneously see design flow at average head. LESSON FOR THE APP: at low head, `P = rho*g*Q*H*eta` fed a published *average* head will NOT reproduce nameplate. Use this plant specifically as the regression test that the app does not over-claim on low-head sites.

### BENCHMARK 3 — Middle Marsyangdi, Nepal (MID HEAD, Francis)
- Installed capacity: **70 MW** (2 x 35 MW Francis)
- Gross head: **108 m**
- Design discharge: **80 m3/s**
- Annual energy: **380 GWh** (power-technology states "The project generated 380 GWh"; ~398 GWh appears elsewhere as the design figure)
- Run-of-river, COD 2008, owned by Nepal Electricity Authority
- SOURCES (STITCHED — flag this): design discharge 80 m3/s and "Total power rating: 78 MW" from Fichtner https://www.fichtner.de/en/projects/detailpage/middle-marsyangdi-run-of-river-hydropower-plant-nepal ; gross head 108 m, 70 MW, 2 x 35 MW Francis, 380 GWh, COD 2008 from https://www.power-technology.com/marketdata/power-plant-profile-middle-marsyangdi-nepal/ ; 2 x 35 MW / 70 MW corroborated at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Marsyangdi_Hydropower_Station
- **Physics check: rho*g*Q*H_gross = 84.76 MW -> implied eta = 0.826 against 70 MW, or 0.920 against Fichtner's 78 MW rating**
- **Capacity factor = 380e3 / (70 * 8760) = 0.620**
- CAVEAT: two capacity figures circulate (70 MW nameplate vs Fichtner's 78 MW "total power rating"). Head is published as gross only; assuming ~10% head loss (net ~97 m) gives eta = 0.92 at 70 MW, which is the physically sensible reading. The 0.62 capacity factor is realistic for a monsoon-driven Himalayan run-of-river scheme with very low dry-season flow — useful for calibrating the app's seasonal expectations.

### BENCHMARK 4 — Ryburg-Schwoerstadt, Switzerland/Germany, High Rhine (LOW HEAD, Kaplan) — PARTIAL
- Installed capacity: **120 MW** (4 x 30 MW vertical, double-regulated Kaplan; 75 rpm, 7000 mm runner, 11 kV)
- Head: **7.6 – 12 m** (published as a range, which is honest for a Rhine ROR plant)
- Annual average energy production: **760 GWh**
- Design discharge: **NOT PUBLISHED on the source page** — I found no citable value and am not asserting one
- SOURCE: ANDRITZ Hydro News 36 — https://www.andritz.com/hydro-en/hydronews/hn36/ryburg-schwoerstadt-switzerland
- **Capacity factor = 760e3 / (120 * 8760) = 0.723**
- Back-solved design flow (DERIVED, not citable): at eta=0.90 and H=12 m, Q = 1133 m3/s. Included only as a plausibility anchor; do not display it in the app.

### HOW TO USE THESE
The span is deliberate: head 8.5 m -> 108 m -> 351.5 m, and flow 7.5 m3/s -> 80 m3/s -> 1500 m3/s. Chilime and Middle Marsyangdi validate the high/mid-head Pelton+Francis regime where `rho*g*Q*H*eta` works well (eta 0.89–0.92 on net head). Rheinfelden and Ryburg validate that the same formula OVERSTATES low-head plants when fed a published average head. Observed capacity factors cluster at **0.62–0.72**, which is the sanity band for a run-of-river annual-energy estimate: if the app produces CF > 0.8 for a run-of-river scheme, it is wrong.

## PART 2 — HOUSEHOLD CONSUMPTION FOR THE "POWERS N HOUSEHOLDS" LINE

**United States — VERIFIED directly from EIA.** 10,791 kWh per residential utility customer per year (2022), about 899 kWh/month. State range: Louisiana 14,774 kWh (highest), Hawaii 6,178 kWh (lowest). Source: https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&t=3

**European Union — PARTIALLY VERIFIED.** Confirmed on the Eurostat page itself: "Electricity consumption per capita in the household sector in the EU in 2023 was 1.5 MWh per capita (1 545 kWh)", ranging from under 1 MWh/capita in Romania, Poland and Latvia to 3.8 MWh in Sweden and 4 MWh in Finland. Source: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Electricity_and_heat_statistics . That page also gives EU gross electricity production 2023 = 2749 TWh and notes hydro fell from 57.0% of renewable electricity in 2010 to 27.1% in 2023.
**CAUTION:** a figure of 3.6 MWh (3,600 kWh) per DWELLING for the EU in 2023, range Romania 1.8 MWh to Sweden 8.5 MWh, is widely attributed to Eurostat, but I could NOT confirm it on the Eurostat pages I fetched — the "Energy consumption in households" page carries only percentage splits by end-use, not absolute per-dwelling kWh. Do not ship the 3,600 kWh figure without pulling it from the Eurostat database tables directly. The 1,545 kWh/capita figure IS safe to cite.

**Nepal / low-consumption regions — NO GOOD SOURCE FOUND.** The only figures I surfaced (~380 kWh/yr per-capita all-sector; household figures of 7 and 119 kWh/month) come from a Kathmandu Post opinion column and the household numbers look internally inconsistent. DO NOT USE. Fix: derive per-capita from the OWID/World Bank data the app already fetches, or take residential sales divided by residential customers from the NEA annual report and vendor it at build time. Note iea.org returns 403 to automated fetches, so IEA country pages are not scrapeable here.

**PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION:** hardcode a small region -> kWh/yr lookup ({US: 10791 per household, EU: 1545 per capita, ...}) with the citation rendered in the UI, and let the user override it. Do not compute it live — none of the probed APIs expose household consumption at all.

## PART 3 — CROSS-CUTTING FINDINGS AND CORRECTIONS TO DOCS

**The viable browser-only stack is exactly three sources, all keyless and all ACAO: \*** — World Bank Indicators (hydro % of electricity, 331 bytes with `mrnev=1`), OWID grapher CSV (hydro generation in TWh by country-year, 234 KB), and WRI GPPD (per-plant capacity + lat/lon + estimated generation, pre-filtered to 2.5 MB). Everything else in this cluster is a dead end.

**CORRECTION — World Bank absolute-energy indicators are gone.** `EG.ELC.HYRO.KH`, `EG.ELC.PROD.KH` and `EN.PRD.ELEC` are all still LISTED in `/v2/indicator` but every data query returns `{"message":[{"id":"175","key":"Invalid format","value":"The indicator was not found. It may have been deleted or archived."}]}`. Only the `.ZS` percentage series serve data. Any doc telling you to fetch hydro kWh from the World Bank is stale — combine WB `EG.ELC.HYRO.ZS` with OWID's absolute generation, or just use OWID for both.

**CORRECTION — the Ember bulk CSV URL is dead.** `https://ember-energy.org/app/uploads/2025/01/yearly_full_release_long_format.csv` now 301s to `/page-not-found/`, and Ember's API requires a key. Use OWID, which republishes Ember data (Entity values literally read e.g. "ASEAN (Ember)").

**CORRECTION — IRENA's API is metadata-only, and its CORS headers actively mislead.** The OPTIONS preflight passes with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type`, and the config endpoint self-reports `"CORS":true`. But PxWeb needs a POST to return observations, and POST returns 404 on all three tables tested while GET on the identical URL returns 200; the `?query=` GET fallback returns 200 and silently ignores the query. IRENA is download-only in practice.

**Two preflight traps, opposite in shape.** (a) World Bank: OPTIONS returns 404 with NO CORS headers, so the app must send ONLY simple requests — adding `X-Requested-With` or a JSON `Content-Type` triggers a preflight and breaks it, even though the ACAO on the GET is `*`. (b) raw.githubusercontent.com: OPTIONS returns 403 but DOES carry `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`; plain unpreflighted GETs work. In both cases: send no custom headers.

**Coverage gaps that actually matter.** Geographic coverage is good everywhere for the national-level sources — WB gives NPL 2023 = 99.09%, GPPD has 12 Nepali / 162 Swiss / 1449 US hydro plants. The real gaps are: (1) GPPD's *measured* `generation_gwh_*` columns are largely empty outside the US/EU so most of the world silently falls back to modelled `HYDRO-V1` estimates; (2) GPPD is frozen at 2017 capacity data; (3) **GPPD has almost nothing below ~1 MW**, which is precisely the size band a run-of-river design tool targets — so it can only support the "compare against a big named plant" framing, never "compare against similar small schemes"; (4) no source here offers sub-national or seasonal resolution.

**Units, stated precisely as observed.** World Bank `EG.ELC.HYRO.ZS` = percent of total electricity production, and the API's own `unit` field is an EMPTY STRING — do not rely on it. OWID grapher `electricity-mix.csv` column `Hydropower` = **TWh**. GPPD `capacity_mw` = MW; `generation_gwh_*` and `estimated_generation_gwh_*` = GWh. Eurostat = MWh/kWh as labelled. Chilime's own site expresses annual energy in both GWh and Nepali "units" (1 unit = 1 kWh).

**Cheapest realistic queries measured.** WB single-country most-recent value = 331 bytes (`?format=json&mrnev=1`), gzip available. OWID grapher hydro CSV = 233,887 bytes, no server-side country filter possible. OWID full energy CSV = 9,229,369 bytes raw / 2,478,108 brotli — too heavy for runtime. GPPD full = 11,973,385 bytes; hydro-only subset = 2,542,655 bytes.

**Rate limits and transport.** None enforced or advertised on World Bank, OWID or raw.githubusercontent during probing (WB sends `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400` behind Cloudflare). IRENA self-documents `maxCalls 10 / timeWindow 10`s, `maxValues 1000`, `maxCells 100000`. EIA sits behind api.data.gov's umbrella (default 1000 req/hr per key). HTTPS worked on every endpoint tested; no TLS or mixed-content issues anywhere.

**Biggest free feature found:** GPPD's per-plant `latitude`/`longitude` alongside `capacity_mw` and `estimated_generation_gwh_2017`. Combined with the user's own site coordinates this yields "your scheme is X% of <named real plant>, Y km away" — far more compelling than a national percentage, at the cost of one build-time-filtered CSV. **Mandatory filter: strip pumped storage**, which GPPD labels `primary_fuel=Hydro` (Bath County 2862 MW, Limmern 1000 MW, Bieudron 1285 MW are all storage/pumped, net energy consumers) and which would otherwise corrupt every comparison.

Attribution required per https://github.com/tilezen/joerd/blob/master/docs/attribution.md (must credit the underlying DEMs actually used — SRTM/NASA, EU-DEM, USGS NED, GMTED, ETOPO1). Tiles are static since 2017 (Last-Modified: Sun, 12 Nov 2017) — dataset is stable but effectively frozen/unmaintained; keep the URL configurable. Path-style s3.amazonaws.com host works today; virtual-host style also exists.
sources.enables: MapLibre hillshade layer + optional 3D terrain exaggeration under the basemap, so head/gradient along a river reads visually — the single most useful map layer for a hydropower site tool.

Open Data under ODbL. https://osm.org/copyright', type='overlay', generator='tippecanoe v2.67.0', vector_layers=[{id:'waterway', fields:{length_m:Number, root_nodeid:Number, root_nodeid_120:Number}, minzoom 0, maxzoom 11}]. notes:
RECOMMENDATION (one stack, all keyless, all CORS-verified live today):

1) BASEMAP — OpenFreeMap, style 'liberty' or 'positron'.
   map style: https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/liberty  (or .../positron)
   It is the only source probed that combines: ACAO '*' everywhere (tiles, style, TileJSON, glyphs, sprites), no key, no registration, an explicit written promise of 'no limits on the number of map views or requests', and a licence with no share-alike trap (ODbL data + open styles, attribution auto-injected by MapLibre).

2) RIVER LAYER — do NOT add a source; it is already in the basemap.
   OpenFreeMap serves the OpenMapTiles schema, so source-layers 'waterway' (class=river/stream/canal/ditch/drain, brunnel, intermittent, name, name:en, name:latin, minzoom 3) and 'water' + 'water_name' are already in every tile you fetch. The Liberty style already has waterway_river / waterway_other / waterway_tunnel / waterway_line_label / water_name_line_label. Restyle those seven layers (thicker, saturated blue, labels always on, filter class=='river' vs 'stream') and you get a named river network for zero extra bytes and zero extra requests. This is the cheapest win in the whole cluster.
   Optional second river layer for network topology: WaterwayMap.org PMTiles (https://data.waterwaymap.org/planet-waterway-rivers-etc.pmtiles). Verified 206 ranged GET with ACAO '*' AND — critically — a passing OPTIONS preflight that allows the 'range' header (204, Access-Control-Allow-Headers: range). Its 'root_nodeid' and 'length_m' attributes let you highlight an entire connected river system and filter by total network length. Mirror the file to your own R2/S3 before shipping; the planet archives are 0.7–2.6 GB and hotlinking someone's hobby bucket is rude even with range reads.

3) HILLSHADE / TERRAIN — AWS Terrain Tiles, terrarium encoding.
   source: { type:'raster-dem', tiles:['https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png'], tileSize:256, encoding:'terrarium', maxzoom:15 }
   ACAO '*' plus a clean OPTIONS 200. Global to z15 (z16 = 404). Real DEM values in METRES, so the same source drives a hillshade layer, 3D terrain, and any client-side head/gradient computation for a hydropower site. The 'x-amz-meta-x-imagery-sources' header is CORS-exposed and names the exact DEM per tile (Nepal→SRTM+GMTED, Switzerland→EU-DEM, US→1/9 arc-sec NED) — free provenance for a data-sources panel.

WHAT TO AVOID AND WHY (all verified, not assumed):
- tile.openstreetmap.org: works and is ACAO '*', and a hobby app IS permitted, but the policy (fetched live) forbids any prefetch/offline/'download area' feature, requires a non-stripped Referer (so no restrictive Referrer-Policy meta tag), and says blocking happens 'without notice' with 'no SLA or guarantee'. Fine as a user-selectable fallback layer; wrong as the default for a map-heavy app.
- CARTO: technically wide open (ACAO '*') but CARTO's own docs restrict the basemap service to Enterprise licensees and non-profit grantees. Licence risk, no functional gain over OpenFreeMap Positron.
- Esri server.arcgisonline.com and basemaps.arcgis.com: everything works keylessly with ACAO '*' (imagery 20,740 B/tile, World_Hillshade 9,637 B/tile, full vector style+fonts+sprites), but Esri required migration to the token-gated ibasemaps-api service by 30 Apr 2022. Keyless production use is outside their ToU. Acceptable as an opt-in 'Satellite' toggle if the team accepts that risk; not the default.
- Stadia/Stamen 401, MapTiler 403 — both key-gated, disqualified by the brief.

CORRECTIONS TO COMMONLY-CITED DOCS (each observed, not inferred):
- Protomaps demo-bucket.protomaps.com/v4.pmtiles serves 206 ranged responses to curl but returns NO Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and its OPTIONS preflight returns 403. It is a hard dead end for a browser-only app on another origin, despite being the URL in most PMTiles demos (those demos are same-origin or use their own buckets). api.protomaps.com is 403 without a key. Protomaps runs no free public planet PMTiles host — the Protomaps route means self-hosting your own extract.
- tiles.wmflabs.org (the classic free hillshade overlay) no longer resolves in DNS. Dead.
- OSM-FR 'openriverboatmap' now 302-redirects to https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png, i.e. the waterway-styled raster layer is gone and anyone still using that URL is unknowingly loading standard OSM tiles under the OSM tile policy. (a.tile.openstreetmap.fr/hot/ IS still alive, 200 + ACAO '*'.)
- Esri Reference/World_Hydro_Reference_Overlay does not exist on services.arcgisonline.com — 404. The Reference folder holds only World_Boundaries_and_Places, World_Boundaries_and_Places_Alternate, World_Reference_Overlay, World_Transportation.
- maps.wikimedia.org returns a 403 that explicitly restricts tiles to Wikimedia and affiliated sites.

PMTILES / RANGE-REQUEST MECHANICS (the thing that actually decides self-hosting):
A cross-origin PMTiles read sends a Range header, which is NOT CORS-safelisted, so it ALWAYS triggers an OPTIONS preflight. Two hosts passed both halves: data.waterwaymap.org (204, allow-headers: range) and pmtiles.io (206 + ACAO '*'). GitHub Pages serves 206 with 'Accept-Ranges: bytes' and 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *', so a PMTiles extract shipped in the same repo as the static site works with no CORS at all — but GitHub Pages caps a single file at 100 MB and the site at 1 GB, so only a country/basin extract fits. For anything bigger use Cloudflare R2/S3 and configure the bucket CORS explicitly (allow GET/HEAD, allow the Range request header, expose ETag and Content-Range), then re-run the OPTIONS probe to confirm.

MEASURED PAYLOADS (single realistic request, live): OpenFreeMap MVT z12 Kathmandu 9,784 B gzip / z10 dense-US 190,597 B gzip; OpenFreeMap style liberty 43,079 B, positron 25,153 B; OpenFreeMap glyph range 76,580 B; terrarium DEM z12 31,251 B, z15 96,449 B; OSM PNG z10 51,644 B; Carto light_all z10 26,471 B (@2x voyager 90,657 B); OpenTopoMap z10 53,580 B; Esri imagery z10 20,740 B, Esri hillshade z10 9,637 B; VersaTiles MVT z10 195,685 B; USGSHydroCached z10 14,662 B; USGSShadedReliefOnly z10 8,367 B. Only the vector-tile sources served Content-Encoding: gzip; all raster PNG/JPEG tiles are served unencoded (already compressed).

GAP: nothing keyless was found that serves a hydrologically-attributed global river network (Strahler order, discharge, catchment area) as vector tiles. HydroSHEDS/HydroRIVERS has no keyless hosted tile service — if the app needs order/discharge styling globally, that has to be pre-processed into a self-hosted PMTiles extract. Within the US, hydro.nationalmap.gov NHD/NHDPlus_HR fills the gap and is CORS-open.

sources.gotchas: UNITS: DIS_AVG_LS is LITRES PER SECOND, not m³/s — divide by 1000. CAP_MCM is million cubic metres. AREA_* and CATCH_SKM are km². NODATA SENTINEL is -99 (not blank, not null) — AREA_REP=-99, CAP_MCM=-99, DOR_PC=-99 all mean missing; a naive parseFloat will silently inject -99 into your maths. YEAR_TXT is a STRING like 'Built 1958', sometimes with other prefixes — must be regex-parsed, not Number()'d. File begins with a UTF-8 BOM which will corrupt the first header key ('﻿GDW_ID') unless stripped. Fields contain embedded commas inside quotes (dam names, county lists) so a naive split(',') shifts columns — I saw this produce junk MAIN_USE values like '6', '7', '54102'; use PapaParse or a real RFC4180 parser (the official GDW viewer itself uses PapaParse). MAIN_USE is blank on 79% of records, so 2,214 'Hydroelectricity' is a floor, not a census of hydro dams. HOSTING CAVEAT — THIS IS THE BIG ONE: this URL is the private CDN (Backblaze B2 behind confluv.io) that the official GDW viewer at https://gdw-viewer.web.app/ fetches; I found it by reading the viewer's geojsonStore.6b1cb4df.js bundle. It is NOT a documented public download endpoint. The documented route on https://www.globaldamwatch.org/database is a Google Form (https://forms.gle/uGPPTELE8hEaNMhR7), which a static app cannot automate. Depending on this URL is hotlinking a third party's asset and it can vanish or change hash without notice — mirror the file into your own repo/CDN and re-attribute. LICENCE DISCREPANCY: the GDW site text says 'free CC BY license' but the viewer's own map attribution string says CC BY-SA 4.0 — resolve before shipping. Paper DOI 10.1038/s41597-024-03752-9.

The only routes are a build-time download vendored into your own repo, or a proxy — the latter is excluded by the brief. Vendoring is entirely viable: it is only 667 KB, CC-compatible under ORNL's Data Use Policy (https://hydrosource.ornl.gov/data-use-policy/ — read it, it is not displayed on the dataset page), and updates annually, so a yearly rebuild keeps it fresh. DOCUMENTATION CORRECTION: the old NHAAP (National Hydropower Asset Assessment Program) branding is gone — hydrosource.ornl.gov/dataset/... paths 404; the current pattern is hydrosource.ornl.gov/data/datasets/<slug>/ and the successor products are the EHA Plant/Unit/Generation/Capacity-Factor databases. EHA Plant 2026 DOI 10.21951/EHA_FY2026/3374497.

notes:
BEST DAMS+RESERVOIRS LAYER FOR A STATIC APP — the answer is unambiguous: the GDW v1 consensus database CSV at https://data.confluv.io/file/mapping/gdw_v1.csv. Measured 4,907,721 bytes (4.9 MB), 41,145 dams across 163 countries, CORS reflected-origin so fetch() works, Cache-Control max-age=2592000 so it costs one download per user per month. Pair it with the companion vector tiles at https://data.confluv.io/file/mapping/gdw_polygons_v3/{z}/{y}/{x}.pbf (source-layer GDW_reservoirs, promoteId GDW_ID, maxzoom 13) and you get real reservoir polygons joined to the attribute table by GDW_ID. Nothing else in this cluster comes close: GeoDAR is a 61.8 MB shapefile ZIP, the official NID CSV is 67 MB and CORS-blocked, and GRanD/GOODD no longer exist as standalone downloads.

THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE FREE FIELD I FOUND, and it was not in the brief: GDW's DIS_AVG_LS carries a long-term mean discharge at 40,979 of 41,145 dam sites (99.6% coverage), in LITRES PER SECOND. Combined with CATCH_SKM (positive on 40,352) and reservoir geometry, that means a hydropower app can compute a first-order P = ρgQH estimate at essentially every dam on Earth from the same 4.9 MB file it already downloaded for the map — no gauge lookup, no second API, no coverage gap outside the US. I verified the values are physically sane: Iroquois on the St. Lawrence reads 7,745,819 L/s = 7,746 m³/s, and Koshi Barrage in Nepal reads 1,701,796 L/s = 1,702 m³/s. Also free in the same file: CAP_MCM reservoir capacity on 35,334 records, DOR_PC degree of regulation, YEAR_TXT, and an ORIG_SRC provenance column.

HOSTING CAVEAT YOU MUST ACT ON. Both GDW endpoints are the private CDN (Backblaze B2 behind confluv.io) used by the official GDW viewer at https://gdw-viewer.web.app/. I did not find them documented anywhere — I recovered them by downloading and reading the viewer's JS bundles (the CSV URL is in assets/geojsonStore.6b1cb4df.js, the tile URL in assets/IndexPage.678132a1.js). The documented download route on https://www.globaldamwatch.org/database is a Google Form (https://forms.gle/uGPPTELE8hEaNMhR7), which a static app cannot automate. So: use these URLs to obtain the data now, but mirror the 4.9 MB CSV and the tile pyramid into your own repo or CDN rather than hotlinking a third party's asset in production. Also resolve a licence discrepancy first — the GDW site says "free CC BY license" while the viewer's own map attribution string says CC BY-SA 4.0.

CORRECTIONS TO PUBLISHED DOCUMENTATION, all verified live:
- globaldamwatch.org (bare domain) DOES NOT RESOLVE — curl exit 6, nslookup returns no address. www.globaldamwatch.org works. Most citations in the literature are written without the www and are therefore broken.
- GRanD v1.3 and GOODD are being DISCONTINUED as standalone products; the GDW site states they are "fully integrated into the GDW database". Their content survives inside gdw_v1.csv via ORIG_SRC (GRanD 7,424; GOODD 23,633; GOODD-NID 2,298; GROD 6,060; JRC-GSW 1,426; FHReD 205).
- NID's documented /api/nation/summary and /api/nation/gis both return 400 "Invalid request format"; /api/dams/state/{ST} and /api/dams/search return 404. Only /api/nation/csv works. The non-"sec" host nid.usace.army.mil does not connect at all.
- ORNL's NHAAP branding is retired and hydrosource.ornl.gov/dataset/... paths 404. Current pattern is hydrosource.ornl.gov/data/datasets/<slug>/; the successor products are EHA Plant/Unit/Generation/Capacity-Factor.
- GeoDAR moved off figshare to Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.6163413).
- datasets.wri.org/dataset/globalpowerplantdatabase 301s to /datasets/global-power-plant-database, which serves Cache-Control: private, no-store HTML with no CORS file endpoint. GitHub raw is the only clean browser host for GPPD.

THE NID WORKAROUND IS THE OTHER BIG WIN. The official USACE NID API is a hard dead end — and importantly, it is not a missing-CORS accident but a deliberate origin ALLOWLIST. It returns four Access-Control-* headers (Allow-Credentials, Allow-Headers, Allow-Methods, Max-Age) with NO Access-Control-Allow-Origin for a third-party origin; sending Origin: https://nid.sec.usace.army.mil instead makes ACAO appear echoing that exact value, and the OPTIONS preflight returns 204 with no ACAO. No client-side trick defeats that. But Esri's authoritative republication at services2.arcgis.com/FiaPA4ga0iQKduv3/arcgis/rest/services/NID_v1/FeatureServer/0 serves the same 92,606 dams with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, arbitrary bbox and SQL queries, GeoJSON output and gzip. A Potomac viewport query (166 dams, 8 fields) is 9,396 bytes on the wire. 2,530 records carry "Hydroelectric" in PURPOSES. I found it via the ArcGIS Online search API (which is itself CORS-open); the owner is Esri_US_Federal_Data with 5.09M views. Use this instead of the official NID.

WATCH FOR THIS ARCGIS TRAP: the FeatureServer returns HTTP 200 with ACAO: * even for a bad URL, with an error object in the body — I got '200 OK' plus {"error":{"code":400,"message":"Invalid URL"}} on two guessed service paths and briefly mistook them for working endpoints. Always check for an 'error' key, never trust the status code. Also maxRecordCount is 2000, so wide-area queries silently truncate unless you check exceededTransferLimit and paginate.

BIGGEST LOSS: ORNL's EHA Plant Database FY2026 (667,233 bytes, 2,257 US plants, last modified 2026-07-17) is by far the richest hydropower-specific dataset here — HY_MW, HY_MWh, HY_Pf capacity factor, HY_OpYear, PSH_MW, lat/lon, FERC docket and expiry, EIA_PtID, HUC12, balancing authority — but the S3 bucket has ZERO CORS config and OPTIONS returns 403. Unreachable from a browser. Since the brief forbids a proxy, the practical answer is to VENDOR it at build time: it is only 667 KB and updates annually, so a yearly rebuild keeps it current. Check https://hydrosource.ornl.gov/data-use-policy/ first — the terms are not shown on the dataset page. Note its NODATA sentinel is the literal string 'NA', and HY_Pf/PSH_Pf are percentages (26.15 means 26.15%, not 0.2615).

UNITS, CONFIRMED FROM LIVE RESPONSES NOT ASSUMED. GDW is metric with traps: DIS_AVG_LS is litres/second (divide by 1000 for m³/s), CAP_MCM is million m³, areas are km², and the NODATA sentinel is -99 (not blank, not null) so a naive parseFloat injects -99 into your arithmetic. GDW's YEAR_TXT is a string like "Built 1958", and the file has a UTF-8 BOM that corrupts the first header key. NID/ArcGIS is entirely US customary, quoted verbatim from the live CSV header: "Dam Height (Ft)", "Hydraulic Height (Ft)", "NID Storage (Acre-Ft)", "Max Storage (Acre-Ft)", "Surface Area (Acres)", "Drainage Area (Sq Miles)", "Max Discharge (Cubic Ft/Second)", "Volume (Cubic Yards)". HYDRAULIC_HEIGHT (feet) is the field to use for head, and DRAINAGE_AREA (square miles) joins cleanly to USGS gauge drainage areas for flow scaling.

PARSING WARNING FOR BOTH CSVs: GDW and GPPD both contain commas inside quoted fields. A split(',') approach shifts columns and produces silent garbage — I saw it yield MAIN_USE values of '6', '7' and '54102' before I switched to a real RFC4180 parser. The official GDW viewer uses PapaParse and caches into localForage; copy that pattern.

RECOMMENDED STACK FOR THE APP: (1) GDW CSV, 4.9 MB, mirrored — global dams, reservoirs, mean discharge, the backbone layer. (2) GDW vector tiles — reservoir polygons, joined by GDW_ID. (3) GPPD from GitHub raw, 1.93 MB gzipped — 7,156 existing hydro plants with capacity_mw and coordinates, all 7,156 complete on both, though frozen at v1.3.0 since 2021 so label it as historical. (4) NID via the Esri ArcGIS mirror — on-demand US viewport queries at ~9 KB each, for US detail only. Total baseline payload roughly 7 MB, all cacheable, no key, no proxy, no backend.

COVERAGE HONESTY FOR NON-US USERS: GPPD's non-US hydro coverage is genuinely thin — Nepal has just 12 plants, all from the defunct GlobalEnergyObservatory with no commissioning year and no owner, versus 1,449 for the USA. GDW is far more even (Nepal 26, Switzerland 109, China 8,238, India 7,095) and should be the primary layer outside the US. Within the US, prefer the NID ArcGIS mirror for structural detail and vendored ORNL EHA for generation performance.

Use format=rdb, not json: RDB is 2.3x smaller uncompressed (32 vs 73 bytes/value) and still 12% smaller gzipped, and parses with a split('\n')/split('\t') in a few lines. RDB packs multiple qualifiers colon-separated in one cell ('A:e'), whereas JSON gives a real array (['A','e']). statCd=00003 is daily MEAN; omit it and you may get max/min series too. Values are strings; empty cells mean gaps (e.g. 01646500 has 35,224 values across 35,225 possible days).

notes:
HEADLINE ANSWER (the number the report was commissioned for): A BROWSER CAN BUILD A FULL FLOW-DURATION CURVE FROM THE COMPLETE HISTORICAL RECORD, EASILY. Measured on site 01646500, startDT=1900-01-01, 35,224 daily mean values spanning 1930-03-01 to 2026-08-09 (96 years): format=rdb 1,141,239 bytes raw -> 170,760 bytes ON THE WIRE gzipped; format=json 2,587,328 raw -> 193,024 wire. Second station 06192500 (1900-01-01 onward, 36,196 lines): rdb 1,163,223 raw -> 159,247 wire; json 2,649,299 raw -> 184,012 wire. Fetch completed in 2.5-3.7 s. ~171 KB gzipped is one ordinary HTTP request - smaller than a hero image. Use format=rdb: 32 bytes/value vs 73 for JSON uncompressed, still 12% smaller after gzip, and trivially parsed by splitting on newlines and tabs. No key, no proxy, no backend.

CORS: EVERY endpoint probed in this cluster returned a literal "Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *". Legacy waterservices.usgs.gov additionally sends "Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true" and answers OPTIONS preflight with 200 + Access-Control-Max-Age: 1800 + Allow-Methods: GET. api.waterdata.usgs.gov answers OPTIONS with 200 + Allow-Headers: * + Allow-Methods: DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PATCH, POST, PUT + Max-Age: 600. api.water.usgs.gov (NLDI) answers OPTIONS with 204 + Allow-Methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. There is not a single CORS dead end. HTTPS works everywhere. No API key was required anywhere, and 60 rapid consecutive unkeyed requests to api.waterdata.usgs.gov all returned 200 with no RateLimit-* or Retry-After headers ever appearing.

*** THE ONE THING THAT DOMINATES ARCHITECTURE: waterservices.usgs.gov IS BEING DECOMMISSIONED IN Q1 2027. *** Verified directly from the banner on https://waterservices.usgs.gov/ : "WaterServices will be decommissioned in early 2027. Applications will need to migrate to the APIs hosted at https://api.waterdata.usgs.gov." Corroborating USGS blog/migration material states legacy NWISWeb pages go between October 2026 and February 2027, that decommissioning "may include intentional service degradation and blackouts", and that no intentional degradation begins before August 2026 - i.e. degradation can start ANY TIME NOW (today is 2026-08-11). Practical consequence: the cheap 171 KB RDB full-record pull is on a ~5-7 month clock. Build the data layer behind an adapter interface with two backends from day one, ship legacy-first for the bandwidth win, and be ready to flip to /ogcapi/v0/collections/daily - which costs 1,234,615 wire bytes for the identical 35,224 records, 7.2x more. That 7x regression is the single biggest engineering consequence of the migration and should be budgeted for now.

FOUR SEPARATE HOSTS need CSP connect-src entries, which is easy to get wrong: (1) waterservices.usgs.gov - legacy iv/dv/site/stat; (2) nwis.waterservices.usgs.gov - the 301 target for HISTORICAL iv queries; (3) api.waterdata.usgs.gov - new OGC API + new statistics API; (4) api.water.usgs.gov - NLDI basins/navigation. Note (2) is a genuine trap: ANY iv request carrying startDT/endDT 301-redirects cross-host. I verified the 301 itself carries ACAO: * and so does the target, so fetch() follows it transparently today - but a restrictive CSP would silently break every historical query. Note also (3) api.waterDATA vs (4) api.WATER - two confusingly similar domains that are different services.

UNITS, CONFIRMED FROM LIVE RESPONSES, NOT ASSUMED: discharge is CUBIC FEET PER SECOND. Legacy exact path value.timeSeries[i].variable.unit.unitCode = "ft3/s" (no caret); variableDescription = "Discharge, cubic feet per second"; variableName = "Streamflow, ft³/s". WARNING: variableName is HTML-entity-encoded (³ is superscript 3) and will render literally as "ft³/s" if injected as text - use variableDescription or decode it. The NEW API uses a DIFFERENT string: unit_of_measure = "ft^3/s" (with caret). Any code that string-matches units must accept both. Gage height 00065: unitCode = "ft", "Gage height, feet". Drainage area drain_area_va = 11560.0 is in SQUARE MILES (multiply by 2.58999 for km2), consistent with ft3/s. NLDI navigation distance, by contrast, is in KILOMETRES - the one metric parameter in an otherwise US-customary ecosystem. Values arrive as STRINGS everywhere ("2900", not 2900) and must be parseFloat'd; -999999.0 is the no-data sentinel.

QUALIFIER / APPROVAL CODES OBSERVED LIVE. Across the full 01646500 daily record the actual distribution was: A (approved) 34,762; A+e (approved AND estimated) 227; P (provisional) 123; A+R (approved, revised) 112. Descriptions come back inline: A = "Approved for publication -- Processing and review completed."; P = "Provisional data subject to revision."; e = "Value has been estimated."; R = "Records for these data have been revised." REPRESENTATION DIFFERS BY FORMAT - a real parsing trap: JSON gives a proper array (qualifiers: ["A","e"]) whereas RDB packs them COLON-SEPARATED into one cell ("A:e"), so you must split(':') on the _cd column. The new OGC API replaces letter codes with words: approval_status: "Approved" (and "approved" lowercase in the statistics API). Live IV data is essentially all P - every single current reading at 01646500 carried ["P"]. I could NOT find any "Ice" qualifier: I checked four northern stations (05082500, 05054000, 06934500, 05211000) over 2015-2020 and the only codes present were A, A:R, A:e, P, P:e. Ice affection appears to be handled by estimation (the 'e' flag) rather than a distinct Ice code in modern DV output - 05054000 had 694 A:e days and 05211000 had 915, heavily winter-weighted, which is the ice signature. Practical rule: treat 'e' as reduced-confidence and 'P' as subject-to-revision; never build a firm-energy guarantee on P data.

STATION WITH NO DISCHARGE RECORD - real example and actual response: site 01646580 (POTOMAC RIVER AT CHAIN BRIDGE) has no continuous discharge. Asking IV for 00060 returns HTTP 200 (not an error) with a fully-formed envelope whose timeSeries array is EMPTY: {"name":"ns1:timeSeriesResponseType",...,"value":{"queryInfo":{...},"timeSeries":[]},"nil":false,...}. Asking DV for 00060 over the full POR returns HTTP 200 with an 81-byte body. So the failure mode is a 200 with zero series - you must check timeSeries.length, because res.ok is true and JSON.parse succeeds. Its series catalog shows only dv 80154/80155 (1978-1981) and a long list of qw water-quality series - no 00060 dv at all.

DISCONTINUED STATION - real example and a genuinely dangerous trap: site 01645200 (WATTS BRANCH AT ROCKVILLE, MD), listed under siteStatus=inactive. Its DV full-POR query returns HTTP 200 and 352,415 bytes of perfectly good historical data from 1957-10-01 to 1987-09-29 (10,986 lines, ending "USGS 01645200 1987-09-29 2.80 A:e"). Passing siteStatus=all made NO difference to the DV response (both 352,415 bytes) - historical DV is served regardless of station status. THE TRAP IS THE IV SERVICE: querying IV for this discontinued station returns HTTP 200 with timeSeries.length == 1 and ONE value - {"value":"5.20","qualifiers":["A"],"dateTime":"1984-04-01T23:58:00.000-05:00"}. There is NOTHING in the response marked "discontinued"; the default IV mode is LATEST, and for a dead station "latest" means its last reading ever, 42 years stale. A naive "current flow" widget will confidently display 5.20 ft3/s as live. MITIGATION: always compare the returned dateTime against now and refuse to label anything older than ~6 hours as current, and/or filter station lists with siteStatus=active up front.

EMPTY-RESULT SEMANTICS ARE INCONSISTENT ACROSS THE CLUSTER and this will bite: legacy /nwis/site/ returns HTTP 404 WITH A ZERO-LENGTH BODY when nothing matches (both the Nepal and Switzerland bBoxes did exactly this) - fetch() does not throw on 404, so an unguarded res.json() throws a confusing SyntaxError instead of a clean "no stations". Legacy /nwis/iv/ and /nwis/dv/ instead return 200 with an empty timeSeries array. The new OGC API returns 200 with an empty features array. Write one normalisation wrapper that maps 404-empty-body, 200-empty-timeSeries and 200-empty-features onto a single "no data" result.

STRICT PARAMETER VALIDATION on api.waterdata.usgs.gov, discovered the hard way: any unrecognised query parameter yields HTTP 400 {"code":"InvalidQuery","type":"InvalidQuery","description":"At least one requested property wasn't found"}. My first rate-limit stress test appended a cache-busting "&x=N" and got 40 consecutive 400s that looked exactly like throttling but were not - rerunning with a valid varying parameter (offset) produced 60 consecutive 200s. Do not append cache-busters, analytics params, or anything not in the OpenAPI spec. Also: site IDs on the new API are PREFIXED ("USGS-01646500"), not bare ("01646500") as on legacy - and numberMatched came back null on every single query, so total counts for pagination UI are unavailable; page until you get a short page.

DOES THE STAT SERVICE REPLACE CLIENT-SIDE FDC COMPUTATION? NO - and this is a conceptual point worth being explicit about. Both the legacy /nwis/stat/ and the new observationNormals return DAY-OF-YEAR climatology: for each of the 366 calendar days, the distribution of that day's flow across all years of record. That answers "is today's flow normal for August 10th?" It does NOT answer "what fraction of all days exceed 500 cfs?", which is what a flow-duration curve is. You still compute the FDC client-side from the daily record - which is fine, because that record is only ~171 KB gzipped. Use both: stat for the seasonal p10-p90 shaded band behind the live hydrograph, DV for the FDC and firm-energy analysis. Verified the two stat services agree: legacy Jan-1 p50_va = 8890 and new API Jan-1 p50 = 8890.0, identical. Legacy stat is RDB-ONLY - format=json returns HTTP 400 with an HTML Tomcat error page, so you must parse tab-delimited text there. The migration LOSES two percentile levels: legacy offers p05,p10,p20,p25,p50,p75,p80,p90,p95 (9 levels) while the new API offers only 5,10,25,50,75,90,95 (7) - p20 and p80 disappear in 2027.

COVERAGE - THE HARD LIMIT: USGS is UNITED STATES ONLY, with no partial or degraded international coverage to fall back on. Both non-US probes returned HTTP 404 with empty bodies: Nepal (bBox=85.2,27.6,85.4,27.8) and Switzerland (bBox=8.4,47.4,8.6,47.6). The US probe (bBox=-77.3,38.8,-77.0,39.0) returned 51 stations. For an open-source hydropower tool with any international ambition this cluster covers the US leg only and a completely separate source cluster is required for everywhere else - GRDC, Copernicus/EFAS, national hydrological services, or GloFAS. Worth noting the new monitoring-locations collection does include non-USGS US agencies (the first bbox hit was Maryland Dept of the Environment, agency_code MD007), so filter by site_type_code=ST and check agency if you specifically want USGS-quality streamflow.

BEST FREE FEATURES FOUND (fields that ride along on requests you are making anyway): (1) drain_area_va = 11560.0 sq mi from siteOutput=expanded - unlocks area-normalised flow transfer to ungauged sites, the single most useful field for hydropower. (2) count_nu from seriesCatalogOutput exactly matched the 35,224 values the DV service actually returned, so you can pre-compute download size and show a progress estimate before committing. (3) The new time-series-metadata 'thresholds' array contains real engineering reference values - {"Name":"Base discharge","ReferenceValue":45000}, {"Name":"Begin low flow measurements","ReferenceValue":2000,"SecondaryReferenceValue":2500}, and on the peak series {"Name":"Highest since 1889-01-01","ReferenceValue":484000} - free flood-stage and low-flow context lines for charts. (4) data_gap_interval "PT1H15M" (ISO-8601) tells you the expected sampling interval so you can render genuine gaps instead of drawing straight lines across them. (5) The peaks collection provides water_year as a first-class field, so no Oct-Sep arithmetic. (6) Every IV/DV response embeds siteName, lat/lon, HUC, county and full timezone info, so one multi-site call populates an entire map layer with no second metadata request. (7) NLDI comid/position turns an arbitrary map click into an NHDPlus reach, the foundation for ungauged-site support.

CHEAPEST HIGH-VALUE CALL IN THE CLUSTER: the multi-site IV query. Maryland statewide latest discharge returned 201 live gauge series - each with name, coordinates, current value, timestamp and qualifier - for 300,256 raw / 13,586 bytes on the wire. A national live-streamflow map is a handful of gzip requests. A bBox variant returned 57 series for 4,318 bytes.

RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE: (a) discovery via /nwis/site/ bBox with hasDataTypeCd=dv&siteStatus=active, then siteOutput=expanded for drainage area and seriesCatalogOutput for period of record; (b) live panel via multi-site IV bBox, with a staleness guard on dateTime to defeat the discontinued-station trap; (c) FDC and firm energy from the full-POR DV RDB pull at ~171 KB, computed and cached in IndexedDB - it is immutable history apart from the provisional tail, so cache it hard and only re-fetch the last ~60 days; (d) seasonal band from /nwis/stat/ daily (46 KB); (e) design flood from the OGC peaks collection; (f) basin polygon from NLDI when the user wants the map visual. Put all of it behind one adapter with legacy and OGC implementations, because (a)-(d) all die in Q1 2027.

The streamflow column is frequently EMPTY (both the first and last rows of the station I extracted end in a trailing comma) — you must handle sparse targets. THE METHOD, verified: (1) GET Range bytes=-65536 to grab the tail; find PK\x06\x06 (ZIP64 EOCD) — I read total entries 13,815, central-directory size 1,871,633, CD offset 12,513,685,669. (2) GET Range for the 1.87 MB central directory once and cache it; parse PK\x01\x02 records, honouring the 0x0001 ZIP64 extra field for 8-byte csize/usize/local-header-offset. (3) GET Range over [localHeaderOffset, +30+nameLen+extraLen+compressedSize]; skip the 30-byte PK\x03\x04 local header plus name/extra; inflate the raw deflate. I ran exactly this and recovered 3,172,530 characters of valid CSV. Caveat: the CD parse costs 1.87 MB on first load, so cache it in IndexedDB. notes:
BOTTOM LINE FOR A STATIC BROWSER-ONLY APP

Genuinely usable, key-free, CORS-open (build on these):
1. CEMS GFM GeoServer WMS at geoserver.gfm.eodc.eu — the standout find. Global Sentinel-1 observed flood extent, daily time dimension 2015-01-01 through 2026-08-10, ACAO *, GetMap PNG overlays (~400 B to ~7 KB) AND GetFeatureInfo point queries (~200 B) returning a numeric GRAY_INDEX. This is the closest thing in the whole Copernicus/JRC estate to a real hydrology API you can call from a static page.
2. GDACS (JRC) at www.gdacs.org/gdacsapi — ACAO *, GeoJSON, and its flood events carry "source":"GLOFAS". This is the ONLY key-free browser-reachable path to a GloFAS-derived signal anywhere in this cluster.
3. JRC Global Surface Water XYZ tiles on Google Cloud Storage — ACAO *, 2–12 KB PNGs, six layers, verified global to zoom 13.
4. Caravan v1.2 per-station slices out of the 12.5 GB Zenodo ZIP by HTTP range read — verified end-to-end, three requests, ~3 MB, 40 years of daily data.

Hard dead ends (do not spend time here):
- Copernicus CDS GloFAS/EFAS reanalysis. DEFINITIVE: no key-free endpoint returns data. POST .../processes/cems-glofas-historical/execution -> 401 "authentication required"; GET /api/retrieve/v1/jobs -> 401. The irony is that CDS's CORS is *perfectly* permissive — the preflight echoes any header you ask for, including private-token and authorization — so the browser is not the obstacle; the account is. Even with a key it fails a static-app design on four counts: the key is public in your JS, jobs are asynchronously queued, output is NetCDF/GRIB, and the smallest unit of retrieval is a gridded subset file rather than a point series.
- GRDC. No CORS on any host, no REST API at all, and the delivery model is literally "a download link will be sent within 24 hours to the email address you entered." Not automatable from a browser under any circumstances.
- GSIM data files. The metadata at doi.pangaea.de reflects Origin and looks promising, but store.pangaea.de — where the 84 MB and 888 MB zips actually live — returns no ACAO at all. Classic CORS split; easy to waste an afternoon on.
- GloFAS-IS / EFAS web portal API. I decompiled the live 431 KB React bundle to find the real endpoints (/api/wms/, /api/fms/vectortile/{product}/RepPoints/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf, /api/fms/legends-v2/glofas/...). Every one 404s unauthenticated. The blanket ACAO * from their nginx is misleading — the wall is a Django session cookie behind a manual GloFAS-IS registration.

CORRECTIONS TO PUBLISHED DOCS
- GSW tile template: the official site publishes .../maptiles/occurrence/{default}/{z}/{x}/{y}.png. The literal token "default" 404s. Drop the segment entirely. Verified both ways.
- GSW has a newer 2024 release in a differently-named bucket: storage.googleapis.com/water-world/tiles2024/... (note "extent" is renamed "max_extent" there). Discovered by scraping the official viewer; prefer it over the 2021 set.
- CDS STAC catalogue does NOT contain the CEMS collections. /api/catalogue/v1/collections?limit=500 returns 142 collections and grepping for '"id":"cems' finds zero; /collections/cems-glofas-historical is a 404. GloFAS exists in /retrieve/v1/processes but not in the STAC catalogue.
- GDACS EVENTS4APP silently IGNORES ?eventtypes=FL — I asked for floods and got wildfires, earthquakes and cyclones. Use the SEARCH endpoint with eventlist=FL and a date range, which does filter.
- GFM GeoServer has WFS DISABLED ("Service WFS is disabled"), so no GeoJSON vector extraction — WMS raster + GetFeatureInfo only.
- Stale GRDC URLs: /downloads/stationbasics.zip and /SharedDocs/ExterneLinks/GRDC/eng/grdc_stations_zip.html both 404.
- Caravan's current version (v1.6) ships as a 24.8 GB .tar.gz. Gzip streams are not randomly seekable, so the range-slicing technique only works on v1.2's Caravan.zip. Pin to record 7944025 deliberately, and document why, or a future maintainer will "helpfully" upgrade and break it.

UNITS — the specific point raised in the brief
None of the sources in this cluster report discharge in cubic feet per second. Caravan's `streamflow` column is normalised to mm/day over the catchment (area in km2, given separately in attributes_other_*.csv) — this is a per-unit-area depth, not a volumetric rate, and converting to m3/s requires the catchment area. GloFAS itself would report m3/s but is unreachable without a key. GFM returns a raster class index (GRAY_INDEX), not a flow. GSW tiles are pre-rendered colours with no numeric values at all. If the app needs cfs anywhere, it will have to come from a different cluster (USGS).

COVERAGE GAPS WORTH FLAGGING EARLY
Caravan v1.2 covers US, Canada, Brazil, Chile, GB, Australia and the Alps — and essentially nothing in Nepal, South Asia, China, SE Asia or most of Africa. If the app targets global or Himalayan hydropower, Caravan will look impressive in the US and be empty exactly where it matters. GFM WMS and the GSW tiles, by contrast, are genuinely global — I verified 200 responses at Potomac (38.95,-77.12), Nepal (27.7,85.3) and Switzerland (47.5,8.5) for both.

PERFORMANCE NOTES
Two payloads will hurt if fetched naively: the GFM WMS GetCapabilities is 2,256,959 bytes of uncompressed XML (the time dimension enumerates every date since 2015), and GDACS getgeometry is 967,169 bytes per flood polygon. Neither server compresses — I confirmed GDACS ignores Accept-Encoding: gzip, br and still returns Content-Length: 134859 on the event list. Cache the capabilities, fetch polygons lazily on click. Zenodo is the only source advertising an explicit rate limit: 133 requests per 60 s for anonymous callers, exposed via x-ratelimit-limit / x-ratelimit-remaining / x-ratelimit-reset.
