notes:
RANKING BY (BROWSER-USABLE x DATA QUALITY)

TIER 1 — build on these, no reservations:
1. UK EA Hydrology API (England). Best in cluster. Keyless, ACAO: *, gzip, and the only source that ships per-reading QUALITY and COMPLETENESS flags. 18 years of daily mean flow = 6,492 readings in 63 KB gzipped. 1,102 flow stations.
2. Hubeau v2 (France). Keyless, ACAO: *, best compression measured anywhere (540 KB -> 11.9 KB, ~45x). 6,466 stations / 4,150 active, 53k+ daily records at major stations, native radius and bbox search. Only demerit is the litres-per-second trap.
3. Canada GeoMet (api.weather.gc.ca). Keyless, ACAO: *, clean OGC API-Features, 8,057 stations, real-time + full HYDAT archive, and DRAINAGE_AREA_GROSS comes free — which is exactly the field you need for specific-discharge scaling and which USGS makes you fetch separately.
4. PEGELONLINE (Germany). Trivial to implement, excellent compression, free low/normal/high regime classification and a real gauge datum. Demoted below Canada only because just 92 of 787 stations report discharge and there is no historical archive (~30 days).

TIER 2 — usable with real friction:
5. UK EA Flood-Monitoring — trivial, live, but self-declared "Beta / version 0.9".
6. Brazil ANA telemetriaws1 — genuinely keyless with CORS and gives discharge+stage+RAINFALL together, but XML, no gzip (0.9 MB per station-month), and station discovery is broken.

TIER 3 — key required, CORS fine:
7. Norway NVE HydAPI — 401 without a key; CORS and rate-limit headers are exemplary. Shipping the key in static JS is the blocker, not CORS.
8. Nepal DHM — metadata open, values key-gated.
9. Copernicus CDS — catalogue open, data behind token + async job queue.

TIER 4 — dead ends for browser-only:
10. Switzerland hydrodaten.admin.ch — no ACAO, and only a Plotly figure object to scrape.
11. Canada wateroffice + MSC Datamart — no ACAO (use GeoMet).
12. Australia BoM — 403 at the Akamai edge from this network.
13. NZ — no national service; regional Hilltop servers only, one already returning 522.
14. Chile DGA — snia.mop.gob.cl/repositoriodga/ returned 404; no current endpoint found.
15. India-WRIS — no response at all; UNTESTED, not proven dead.

GENUINELY COVERED vs DEAD ENDS
Genuinely covered, keyless, browser-direct: England, France, Germany (federal waterways only), Canada, Brazil (if you supply station codes).
Covered only with a key: Norway, Nepal (metadata only).
Dead ends: Switzerland, Australia, Chile, Scotland/Wales/N.Ireland, pan-European gauges.
Unknown: India.

DOCUMENTATION CORRECTIONS FOUND
- MSC Datamart: the commonly cited https://dd.weather.gc.ca/hydrometric/ now 404s. Current working path is https://dd.weather.gc.ca/today/hydrometric/csv/{PROV}/hourly/ (mirror: hpfx.collab.science.gc.ca). Neither has CORS.
- Hubeau: the documented grandeur_hydro_elab=QmJ is REJECTED with a Pattern validation error. Working values observed live: QmnJ, QmM, HIXnJ, HIXM. The v1 API path now returns 403 Forbidden; v2 is mandatory.
- Brazil ANA: the documented statusEstacoes=T throws System.FormatException (leaking a server source path); numeric values are accepted but return zero station rows regardless.
- Nepal: dhm.gov.np has no API. The real machine-readable service is hydrology.gov.np/gss/api, which I found only by pulling the endpoint out of the SPA's JS bundle (/static/js/main.6cdcf5af.js). This does not appear to be publicly documented anywhere.

CROSS-CUTTING UNIT WARNING — the single biggest correctness risk in this cluster
Every agency uses a different convention and several ship NO unit field at all:
- Hubeau France: discharge in LITRES PER SECOND, levels in mm, and NO unit field anywhere. Verified twice against physical plausibility (Rhone at Lyon 349000 = 349 m3/s; Saone 1519253 = 1519 m3/s). Divide by 1000.
- UK EA: m3/s, but the unit lives INSIDE THE MEASURE ID STRING ('...-m3s-...'), not in a field. Period is in seconds.
- PEGELONLINE: level in CENTIMETRES (unit field present and correct), discharge m3/s.
- Canada: m3/s and metres (unit not in payload; taken from collection metadata).
- Brazil: Vazao m3/s, Nivel cm, Chuva mm.
Confirmed live, as instructed: USGS-style cubic FEET per second appears NOWHERE in this national cluster — every source here is metric. Do not carry a ft3/s assumption over from the USGS work.

METHODOLOGY NOTE AND ONE SELF-CORRECTION
I initially recorded Brazil's telemetriaws1 as having NO ACAO because I piped headers through `head -10` and the access-control lines fell below the cut. Re-running with a full `grep -i access-control` over the complete header dump showed 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' is in fact present. I then re-verified Switzerland, BoM, Chile and NZ the same way to make sure no other verdict was truncation-induced — Switzerland and BoM are confirmed genuinely ACAO-absent. Every ACAO string reported above is copied from actual observed output.

SECOND CAVEAT ON NEGATIVE RESULTS: BoM (403 from Akamai) and India-WRIS (total timeout) are both consistent with datacenter-IP filtering on this network rather than deliberate policy. I have marked them DEAD_OR_MOVED and UNCLEAR respectively rather than BLOCKED_NO_CORS, because I did not observe a CORS decision in either case. Both deserve a re-probe from a real residential browser before being written off.

PRIVACY FLAG: the Nepal /gss/api/station payload (45 MB, fully public, CORS-open) contains named individuals with personal mobile numbers in the "Weather Observer's Name" and "Weather Observer Contact No." metadata fields. If that dataset is ingested, strip those fields before displaying or re-hosting.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION
Ship England (EA Hydrology), France (Hubeau), Canada (GeoMet) and Germany (PEGELONLINE) as the keyless browser-direct set — all four are fast, gzipped, and carry enough free metadata (drainage area, river name, datum, period of record, quality flags) that no secondary lookup is needed. Add Brazil only if you pre-bundle a station-code list. Everything else needs either a key, a proxy, or a re-test.

Observed on CARO2/TDAO3: lid="CARO2"; usgsId="07301500"; reachId="13756121" (NHDPlus COMID — this is the free USGS↔NWM join key); name="North Fork of the Red River near Carter"; description="USGS Gaging Station"; latitude=35.168108; longitude=-99.507313; state={abbreviation:"OK",name:"Oklahoma"}; county="Beckham"; timeZone="CST6CDT"; rfc={abbreviation:"ABRFC",name:"Arkansas-Red Basin RFC"}; wfo={abbreviation:"OUN",name:"Norman"}; pedts={observed:"HGIRG",forecast:"HGIFF"} (SHEF parameter codes); status.observed={primary:5.01,primaryUnit:"ft",secondary:0.0107,secondaryUnit:"kcfs",floodCategory:"no_flooding",validTime:"2026-08-11T00:30:00Z"}; flood={stageUnits:"ft",flowUnits:"cfs",categories:{major:{stage:18,flow:-9999},moderate:{stage:17},minor:{stage:16},action:{stage:14}}}; flood.crests.historic[] = full historic peak record, e.g. {occurredTime:"1995-06-04T18:00:00Z",stage:20.08,flow:34800,preliminary:"R",olddatum:false} back to 1959 — a free partial-duration flood series; datums.vertical.value[]={label:"North American Vertical Datum of 1988",abbrev:"NAVD88",description:...}; upstreamLid="SAYO2" and downstreamLid="ALTO2" (free gauge-network topology); inService={enabled:true,message:""}; forecastReliability="Forecasts are issued routinely year-round."; dataAttribution[]={abbrev:"USGS",url:"https://waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis/inventory/?site_no=14105700"}; images.probability.weekint.flow="https://water.noaa.gov/resources/probabilistic/exceedance/CARO2.QINE.prob.weekint.gif" (pre-rendered exceedance-probability plots); plus normalThreshold, lowThreshold, inundation, hydronotes, impactsLowWaters, ObservedFloodCategory, ForecastFloodCategory.
sources.gotchas: UNIT TRAP — three different flow units coexist in one API and you must read the unit field, never assume: status.observed.secondaryUnit="kcfs" (THOUSANDS of cubic feet per second — 0.0107 kcfs = 10.7 cfs), while flood.flowUnits="cfs" and the /reaches NWM series report units="ft³/s". Confirmed live, not assumed. SENTINELS: -999 means 'no value' in status (e.g. TDAO3 status.observed.secondary=-999 with secondaryUnit still "kcfs"; forecast block shows primary:-999, primaryUnit:"", floodCategory:"fcst_not_current", validTime:"0001-01-01T00:00:00Z"); -9999 means 'no value' in flood.categories[].flow. Treat both as null. datums can be an empty shell — TDAO3 returned datums={"vertical":{"value":[]},"horizontal":{"value":[]}} while CARO2 was populated, so datum availability is per-gauge. normalThreshold/lowThreshold are null on some gauges and {value:0,units:"ft"} on others. Many gauges are stage-only: floodCategory:"not_defined" and secondary:-999 means no discharge is published at all.
sources.enables: One call converts a USGS site number or NWS LID into the NHDPlus COMID, lat/lon, NAVD88 datum, flood thresholds and a decades-long historic crest list — letting a browser-only app join USGS observations to National Water Model forecasts with zero backend.

sources.gotchas: CRITICAL: the list response is TRIMMED — item keys are exactly ['lid','name','rfc','wfo','state','latitude','longitude','pedts','status']. reachId and usgsId are NOT present (verified programmatically: 'has reachId? False', 'has usgsId? False'). Getting the COMID requires a second call to /gauges/{lid}, so coordinate→reach is a 2-hop. SRID IS EFFECTIVELY MANDATORY: the spec default is SRID_UNSPECIFIED and omitting srid returned an 18-byte empty result for the same box that returns 83 gauges with srid=EPSG_4326. Always pass srid=EPSG_4326 (enum: SRID_UNSPECIFIED | EPSG_3857 | EPSG_4326). The parameter names use literal dots — bbox.xmin, not bbox[xmin]. DO NOT call /nwps/v1/gauges without a bbox: the unfiltered list is 13,062,808 bytes (12,827 gauges) uncompressed and took over 120 s in my test — it must be run in the background. There is no pagination and no fields/limit parameter. An optional catfim=boolean filter exists (default false).
sources.enables: Draw a live map layer of every NWS forecast gauge in the current viewport, with current stage and flood status, in one uncached request — the coordinate entry point for the whole app.

sources.otherCorsHeaders: Vary: Origin
sources.preflightResult: 204 No Content, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET
sources.contentEncoding: NONE (uncompressed)
sources.rateLimit: None observed
sources.coverage: CONUS NHDPlus v2 reaches (~2.7M). Works for UNGAUGED reaches — this is the key to modelled flow anywhere on the CONUS stream network, not just at gauges.
sources.freeFields: reachId="4508886"; name="Little Falls Branch"; latitude=38.948; longitude=-77.1126; streamflow=["short_range","long_range","medium_range_blend","medium_range","analysis_assimilation"] (tells you which series exist BEFORE you fetch them — use this to avoid wasted calls); route.upstream=[{reachId:"4508760",streamOrder:"2"},{reachId:"4508774",streamOrder:"2"}]; route.downstream=[{reachId:"4509378",streamOrder:"2"}]. streamOrder is a free Strahler order — a decent first-pass proxy for river size when screening hydropower sites.
sources.gotchas: Invalid reach IDs do NOT 404 cleanly — 99999999999 returned HTTP 500 with {"code":13,"message":"Internal server error"}, and 11908224 also returned 500. Client code must treat 500 as 'no such reach' rather than as an outage, and must not retry-storm on it. route only gives immediate neighbours (one hop each way), so walking a river requires N sequential requests — there is no bulk traverse. streamOrder is a STRING ("2"), not a number.
sources.enables: Walk the river network upstream/downstream from any point and get Strahler order for free — lets the app follow a river reach by reach without shipping NHDPlus geometry.

sources.name: NWPS API — National Water Model streamflow forecast by reach (/nwps/v1/reaches/{reachId}/streamflow?series=)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: Vary: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method, Access-Control-Request-Headers
sources.preflightResult: HTTP/1.1 204 No Content; Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET; Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
sources.contentEncoding: NONE — confirmed uncompressed with an explicit 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br' request that produced no Content-Encoding header. Matters a lot here because the unfiltered response is 252 KB.
sources.rateLimit: None observed — 20 rapid sequential GETs all 200, no rate-limit headers, no 429. short_range fetch measured at 0.74 s.
sources.coverage: CONUS NWM domain, gauged and ungauged reaches alike. No coverage outside the US (there is no reach to look up — NLDI returns 404 'No catchment found' for Nepal, so you can never obtain a reachId abroad).
sources.freeFields: Response embeds the full reach object (reach.name, reach.latitude/longitude, reach.route upstream/downstream, reach.streamflow list) so you get metadata + data in ONE request — no need to also call /reaches/{id}. Series payload: {referenceTime:"2026-08-10T22:00:00Z", units:"ft³/s", data:[{validTime:"2026-08-10T23:00:00Z", flow:44.48999786376953}, ...]}. referenceTime is the model init cycle — use it to show data age and to cache-bust correctly. Top-level keys: reach, analysisAssimilation, shortRange, mediumRange, longRange, mediumRangeBlend. mediumRange keys observed = ['mean','member1'..'member6'] (7 traces, mean n=204, members n=240); longRange keys = ['mean','member1'..'member4'] (n=120 each) — FREE ENSEMBLE UNCERTAINTY BANDS, no extra cost.
sources.gotchas: UNITS ARE ft³/s (cubic FEET per second) — confirmed verbatim from the live response field units:"ft³/s", NOT m³/s. Note the character is a UTF-8 superscript three (ft³/s); string-compare carefully. Contrast with the NWM retrospective Zarr on S3, which is m3 s-1 — the same model, different units by access path. ALWAYS PASS ?series= : the bare call returns all five series at 252,639 bytes uncompressed, vs 2,725 bytes for short_range alone — a 93x saving. medium_range alone is 154,466 bytes and long_range 63,359 bytes, both still heavy on mobile. Flows are float32 widened to float64, so values arrive as 44.48999786376953 — round for display. analysisAssimilation came back as an empty object {} on a reach that advertised it in reach.streamflow, so an advertised series is not a guarantee of data; null-check every block. Series enum: analysis_assimilation | short_range | medium_range | long_range | medium_range_blend.
sources.enables: A browser-only 18-hour hourly discharge forecast in ft³/s for ANY CONUS stream reach, gauged or not, with free ensemble spread for 10-day and 30-day horizons — the core hydropower-potential signal.

sources.name: NWPS API — stage-discharge rating curve (/nwps/v1/gauges/{identifier}/ratings)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: Vary: Origin
sources.preflightResult: Not separately probed; same host/CORS config as the other /nwps/v1 paths (204 + ACAO * on /reaches).
sources.contentEncoding: NONE (uncompressed)
sources.rateLimit: None observed; measured 0.74 s
sources.coverage: US gauges that have a published NWS rating. Not universal — stage-only sites and many reservoir/tidal gauges will have no meaningful curve.
sources.freeFields: {stageUnits:"ft", flowUnits:"cfs", data:[{stage:4.24,flow:0},{stage:4.68,flow:2},{stage:4.85,flow:5},{stage:4.96,flow:9},{stage:5.13,flow:16},{stage:5.28,flow:28},{stage:5.44,flow:42},{stage:5.72,flow:70.01},{stage:5.93,flow:93.01},{stage:6.11,flow:118.01},{stage:6.34,flow:151.02},...]}. Note stage=4.24 → flow=0 gives you the effective zero-flow stage (cease-to-flow point) for free.
sources.gotchas: Units here are cfs (plain cubic feet per second), NOT the kcfs used in gauge status and NOT the ft³/s string used by /reaches — three spellings of flow across one API. Only 4.7 KB, so this is cheap to fetch and cache. Curve is a lookup table, not a coefficient form; interpolate between points (log-log is the hydrologically correct interpolation, linear will under-read at low flow). Not every gauge returns a populated curve — check data.length before plotting.
sources.enables: Convert observed stage to discharge client-side, and derive the head/flow relationship at a site — directly usable for hydropower head and flow-duration estimation without any backend computation.

sources.name: NWPS API — observed + forecast stage/flow time series (/nwps/v1/gauges/{identifier}/stageflow[/{product}])
sources.otherCorsHeaders: Vary: Origin
sources.preflightResult: Not separately probed; same host CORS config (204 + ACAO * observed on /reaches).
sources.contentEncoding: NONE — verified with an explicit 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br' GET on this exact URL: response had only 'Vary: Origin', NO Content-Encoding. 228 KB travels raw over the wire.
sources.rateLimit: None observed
sources.coverage: US NWS/USGS gauges. Roughly 30 days of history at 30-minute resolution on the sample gauge.
sources.freeFields: observed={pedts:"HGIRG", issuedTime:"2026-08-11T00:30:00Z", wfo:"OUN", timeZone:"CST6CDT", primaryName:"Stage", primaryUnits:"ft", secondaryName:"Flow", secondaryUnits:"kcfs", data:[{validTime:"2026-07-12T02:00:00Z", generatedTime:"2026-07-12T03:09:36Z", primary:5.25, secondary:0.0251}, ...]}. The self-describing primaryName/primaryUnits/secondaryName/secondaryUnits pairs mean you can label axes correctly without hardcoding. generatedTime vs validTime lets you detect late-arriving/revised values.
sources.gotchas: BIGGEST PAYLOAD IN THE CLUSTER at 233,621 bytes UNCOMPRESSED with no gzip and no date-range parameter — the spec exposes no start/end/period filter, so you cannot ask for less. On a metered mobile connection this is the one call to avoid or to fetch lazily on user action. secondaryUnits is "kcfs" — multiply by 1000 for cfs (0.0251 kcfs = 25.1 cfs). The forecast product can be essentially empty (192 bytes) when floodCategory is "fcst_not_current", which is the common case for non-flooding gauges. /gauges/{id}/stageflow/observed and /products/stageflow/{id}/{pedts} return byte-identical content (216,392) — they are aliases, pick one.
sources.enables: A 30-day observed stage and discharge hydrograph per gauge for flow-duration and baseline-energy analysis, though the payload size makes it a click-to-load rather than a page-load fetch.

sources.freeFields: Authoritative, machine-readable, and complete. The COMPLETE path list is exactly 9 endpoints, all GET: /nwps/v1/gauges, /nwps/v1/gauges/{identifier}, /nwps/v1/gauges/{identifier}/ratings, /nwps/v1/gauges/{identifier}/stageflow, /nwps/v1/gauges/{identifier}/stageflow/{product}, /nwps/v1/monitor, /nwps/v1/products/stageflow/{identifier}/{pedts}, /nwps/v1/reaches/{reachId}, /nwps/v1/reaches/{reachId}/streamflow. Also note the spec has no 'host' or 'basePath' field (both null) — paths in the file already include the /nwps/v1 prefix, so do not concatenate a base path or you will produce /nwps/v1/nwps/v1/... . CRITICALLY: there is NO endpoint that maps a lat/lon to a reachId — /nwps/v1/reaches accepts only a {reachId} path param and 404s as a collection. Confirm the endpoint list from this file rather than from blog posts.

sources.httpStatus: 200 (404 with {"type":"about:blank","title":"Not Found","status":404,"detail":"No catchment found at coords POINT(85.3 27.7)"} outside CONUS)
sources.otherCorsHeaders: Preflight (OPTIONS + Origin + Access-Control-Request-Method: GET) returned HTTP/1.1 204 No Content with 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' and 'Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS'.
sources.preflightResult: 204 No Content; Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *; Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
sources.contentEncoding: Not observed as compressed
sources.rateLimit: None observed; measured 1.00 s
sources.coverage: CONUS NHDPlus v2 catchments only. Verified: POINT(85.3 27.7) [Kathmandu] returns HTTP 404 'No catchment found at coords'. No Nepal, no Europe. Alaska/Hawaii/PR coverage in NHDPlus v2 is partial-to-absent, so treat non-CONUS US as unreliable here even though NWPS gauges exist there.
sources.freeFields: features[0].properties = {identifier:"4508886", navigation:"https://api.water.usgs.gov/nldi/linked-data/comid/4508886/navigation", source:"comid", sourceName:"NHDPlus comid", comid:4508886}. features[0].geometry is a LineString with 30 coordinate pairs — the ACTUAL FLOWLINE GEOMETRY of the reach, free, ready to draw on a map. The returned 'navigation' URL is a self-describing HATEOAS link to upstream/downstream traversal.
sources.gotchas: ANSWERS THE CORE QUESTION: reach-id lookup by coordinate IS possible with NO backend and NO shipped spatial dataset — this endpoint does the point-in-catchment query server-side and returns the COMID. VERIFIED END-TO-END: POINT(-77.12 38.95) → comid 4508886 → https://api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/reaches/4508886 returned 200 {reachId:"4508886", name:"Little Falls Branch", latitude:38.948, longitude:-77.1126} → its short_range series returned units "ft³/s", 18 points, first value flow:44.48999786376953. The whole chain is browser-side. CAVEAT: this is a USGS host, not NOAA — it is a cross-origin dependency on a separate agency, so it is a separate uptime/politics risk. The coords parameter needs WKT with a URL-encoded space (%20) between lon and lat, and it is POINT(lon lat) — LONGITUDE FIRST. A 404 is the normal 'off-network' answer, not an error to retry. It snaps to the nearest catchment's flowline, so a click on a hillside still returns a reach — validate distance before trusting it.
sources.enables: Turns a map click anywhere in CONUS into an NWM reach ID, unlocking modelled streamflow at ungauged sites — the single capability that makes a backend-free hydropower siting app possible.

Basin size scales with the reach: a headwater basin is under 1 KB but a large mainstem basin polygon can be megabytes, so guard on stream order (available free from the NWPS /reaches route.upstream[].streamOrder) before requesting a basin for a high-order reach. sources.freeFields: {metadata:{id:"8594900", name:"Washington", lat:"38.8733", lon:"-77.0217"}, data:[{t:"2026-08-11 01:36", v:"0.671", s:"0.013", f:"0,0,0,0", q:"p"}]}. Station name and coordinates come free in metadata. s = standard deviation of the 1-second samples; q="p" = preliminary (vs "v" verified) — a free data-quality flag; f is a 4-part QC flag string.

All numeric values are STRINGS ("0.671", lat:"38.8733") and must be parseFloat'd. The timestamp t="2026-08-11 01:36" is a space-separated non-ISO string that Safari will not parse with new Date() — replace the space with 'T' and append 'Z' (I requested time_zone=gmt). datum choice materially changes values (NAVD vs MLLW vs STND) and not every station publishes every datum. sources.name: NWM Retrospective v2.1 Zarr on AWS S3 (noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-zarr-pds) — 42-year modelled record
sources.otherCorsHeaders: Content-Length: 9006 on the .zmetadata object. Standard S3 CORS.
sources.preflightResult: Not separately probed; simple GETs need none and ACAO * was present on the actual GET
sources.contentEncoding: Chunks are blosc-compressed inside the payload (not HTTP Content-Encoding)
sources.rateLimit: None observed (public S3, requester does not pay)
sources.coverage: CONUS, 2,776,738 reaches, 367,439 hourly timesteps (~42 years). feature_id .zattrs says 'NHDPlusv2 ComIDs within CONUS, arbitrary Reach IDs outside of CONUS'.
sources.freeFields: Full .zmetadata is only 9,006 bytes and is free to inspect. Arrays available: streamflow, velocity (both shape [367439, 2776738]), plus per-reach coordinate arrays feature_id, latitude, longitude, elevation, order, gage_id (dtype |S15 — a free COMID→USGS gage crosswalk for the whole CONUS network). streamflow/.zattrs = {units:"m3 s-1", scale_factor:0.009999999776482582, add_offset:0.0, missing_value:-999900, long_name:"River Flow"}.
sources.gotchas: CORS IS PRESENT BUT THIS IS A PRACTICAL DEAD END FOR PER-REACH QUERIES — the chunking defeats it. streamflow chunks are [672, 30000] (672 hours x 30,000 reaches). I downloaded chunk streamflow/0.0 and MEASURED 12,565,616 bytes. To extract ONE reach's full 42-year series you must fetch 367,439/672 = 547 chunks at ~12.5 MB each ≈ 6.9 GB, and discard 29,999/30,000 of every byte. Even ONE 28-day window for one reach costs a 12.5 MB download. Do not attempt this client-side. Supporting arrays are also large: latitude/0 = 5,866,481 bytes, feature_id/0 = 794,487 bytes (single-chunk, 2.7M int32); only time/0 is small at 419 bytes. UNIT CONTRAST: retrospective is m3 s-1 (CUBIC METRES per second) whereas the NWPS API reports ft³/s for the same model — 1 m3/s = 35.3147 ft³/s. Values are int32 and REQUIRE decoding as raw*0.01 with -999900 (i.e. -9999.0 after scaling) as missing. Browser use would additionally need a blosc decoder in WASM. Verdict: use only via a server/notebook, or precompute per-site statistics offline and ship a static JSON.
sources.enables: A 42-year modelled flow-duration curve per reach — the ideal hydropower dataset, but only reachable offline; served to the browser it would be a precomputed static file, not a live API call.

notes: BOTTOM LINE: this cluster is a clear GO for a browser-only, key-less, backend-free app — inside the United States. api.water.noaa.gov sends a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every /nwps/v1 endpoint I probed, preflight returns 204 with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET`, no API key, no auth, no observed rate limiting (20 rapid GETs all 200, zero rate-limit headers), and http:// 301-redirects to HTTPS. THE CENTRAL QUESTION — reach lookup by coordinate WITHOUT shipping a spatial dataset — ANSWER: YES, and I verified the whole chain live. The NWPS API itself has NO coordinate→reach endpoint (confirmed against the authoritative swagger.json: /nwps/v1/reaches accepts only a {reachId} path param and the collection path 404s). But USGS NLDI fills the gap and is CORS-enabled: POINT(-77.12 38.95) → https://api.water.usgs.gov/nldi/linked-data/comid/position → comid 4508886 (1,167 bytes, ACAO *, preflight 204 GET/HEAD/OPTIONS) → https://api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/reaches/4508886 → 200, "Little Falls Branch", 529 bytes → .../streamflow?series=short_range → units "ft³/s", 18 hourly points, first flow 44.49, in 2,725 bytes and 0.74 s. So the app can turn a map click into an NWM forecast with three small cross-origin GETs and no NHDPlus shipped. The caveat worth flagging: this puts a hard dependency on a USGS host, a different agency from NOAA, so it is a separate uptime and policy risk than the NOAA API. CORRECTIONS TO COMMONLY-CITED DOCS (all verified): 1. The OpenAPI spec is NOT at /nwps/v1/openapi.json or /nwps/v1/swagger.json — both 404. It is at https://api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/docs/swagger.json (found by reading /nwps/v1/docs/swagger-initializer.js). The spec has null `host` and null `basePath`, and its paths already include /nwps/v1 — concatenating a base path yields a broken /nwps/v1/nwps/v1/... URL. 2. https://api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/ returns 503 from awselb/2.0. This is just "no handler at the version root," not an outage — every child path is healthy. Do not use it as a health check. 3. The bbox parameter is useless without `srid`. The spec default is SRID_UNSPECIFIED, and omitting srid returned an 18-byte empty result for the exact box that returns 83 gauges with `&srid=EPSG_4326`. Always send it. 4. The complete API is 9 GET endpoints, nothing more. THE BIGGEST ENGINEERING CONSTRAINT — NO COMPRESSION ANYWHERE ON api.water.noaa.gov. I explicitly requested `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br` on /gauges/CARO2/stageflow and the response carried only `Vary: Origin` with NO Content-Encoding header. Every byte travels raw. This reshapes the client design: - NEVER call /nwps/v1/gauges unfiltered: 13,062,808 bytes / 12,827 gauges, and it exceeded a 120-second timeout in my test (had to be backgrounded). Always send a bbox. - ALWAYS send ?series= on /reaches/{id}/streamflow: bare = 252,639 bytes vs short_range = 2,725 bytes. A 93x saving from one query param. medium_range is 154,466 and long_range 63,359. - /gauges/{id}/stageflow is 233,621 bytes with NO date-range parameter available — you cannot ask for less. Make it click-to-load, never page-load. Good-news sizes: bbox 0.25°x0.20° = 13,400 bytes in 1.06 s; ratings = 4,713 bytes; reach meta = 529 bytes; NLDI position = 1,167 bytes; NLDI basin = 967 bytes. UNIT REPORTING — I confirmed all of these from live responses rather than assuming, and there is a genuine trap. The SAME API expresses flow three different ways: - /reaches/{id}/streamflow → units:"ft³/s" (cubic FEET per second; the character is a UTF-8 superscript three — string-compare carefully) - /gauges/{id}/ratings and gauge flood.flowUnits → "cfs" - gauge status.secondaryUnit and stageflow secondaryUnits → "kcfs", THOUSANDS of cfs. On CARO2 the live value was secondary:0.0107 kcfs = 10.7 cfs. Rendering that as 0.0107 cfs would be wrong by 1000x. And the NWM Retrospective Zarr on S3 reports the SAME model in "m3 s-1" (metres, not feet) — same model, different units by access path. 1 m3/s = 35.3147 ft³/s. MISSING-VALUE SENTINELS also vary: -999 in gauge status, -9999 in flood.categories[].flow, -999900 raw (= -9999.0 after scale_factor 0.01) in the Zarr. All must be nulled, never plotted. COVERAGE — HARD US-ONLY, which is decisive for an "Opensource hydropower" project with any international ambition. Nepal (84.8,27.2→85.8,28.2) and Switzerland (8.0,47.0→9.0,48.0) both returned literally `{"gauges": []}`. NLDI is blunter: POINT(85.3 27.7) returns HTTP 404 "No catchment found at coords". Puerto Rico returned 114 gauges and Alaska 40, so US territories work for NWPS — but NHDPlus v2 (and therefore NLDI's point→COMID) is CONUS-only, so outside the lower 48 you can find gauges but generally cannot resolve a click to a reach. This cluster cannot serve a non-US site at all; that needs an entirely different source (GloFAS/Copernicus or national agencies). TWO PATHS THAT LOOK OPEN BUT ARE TRAPS — both have valid CORS yet are unusable from a browser because of chunk/file granularity: - NWM Retrospective Zarr: ACAO * confirmed, .zmetadata is a friendly 9 KB — but streamflow chunks are [672, 30000] and I MEASURED one chunk at 12,565,616 bytes. One reach's full 42-year record = 547 chunks ≈ 6.9 GB, discarding 29,999/30,000 of every byte. Even a single 28-day window for one reach costs a 12.5 MB download, plus a WASM blosc decoder. This is the ideal hydropower dataset (42-year flow-duration curves) and it must be precomputed offline into static JSON, not fetched live. - NWM operational NetCDF (noaa-nwm-pds): ACAO * confirmed and the S3 listing is anonymously enumerable, but each channel_rt file is ~13.97 MB and holds all 2.7M reaches for ONE forecast hour. An 18-hour hydrograph for one reach = 252 MB, versus 2,725 bytes from the REST API — a ~100,000x difference. Use the API. STANDOUT FREE FEATURES worth designing around: - /gauges/{identifier} accepts EITHER the NWS LID or the USGS site number (/gauges/07301500 works) and returns usgsId AND reachId together — a free, official USGS↔NHDPlus-COMID↔NWM crosswalk that would otherwise require a lookup table. - /gauges/{id}/ratings is a genuine stage-discharge rating curve in 4.7 KB, including the cease-to-flow point (stage 4.24 → flow 0). Directly usable for stage→discharge conversion client-side. - medium_range returns mean + member1..member6 and long_range mean + member1..member4 — free ensemble uncertainty bands at no extra request cost. - flood.crests.historic[] is a free historic peak series (CARO2 back to 1959, e.g. 1995-06-04 stage 20.08 / flow 34800, with preliminary flags "R"/"O"). - reach route.upstream/downstream include a free Strahler streamOrder (as a STRING, "5") — a cheap first-pass filter for river size before requesting an expensive basin polygon. - Free gauge-network topology via upstreamLid/downstreamLid ("SAYO2"/"ALTO2"), NAVD88 datum metadata, and pre-rendered exceedance-probability GIFs (usable in , since images bypass CORS unless canvas-read). - NLDI throws in the reach's flowline LineString geometry (30 vertices) and an upstream basin POLYGON for 967 bytes — though the basin has NO area attribute, so drainage area must be computed client-side from the polygon. GAPS / ERROR-HANDLING NOTES: invalid reach IDs return HTTP 500 with {"code":13,"message":"Internal server error"} rather than 404 (both 99999999999 and 11908224) — clients must treat 500 as "no such reach" and must NOT retry-storm. Unknown gauge IDs correctly return 404 with a gRPC-style body {"code":5,"message":"[ZZZZ9] could not find gauge ID"}. An advertised series is not a guarantee of data — analysisAssimilation came back as `{}` on a reach that listed it. Per /nwps/v1/monitor, 9,963 of 12,827 gauges are "fcst_not_current" and 4,209 observed are "not_defined": the MAJORITY of gauges have no current forecast, so the UI must degrade gracefully rather than assume data exists. Finally, water.noaa.gov (the HTML site) has NO ACAO header at all — only api.water.noaa.gov is browser-callable; do not plan on scraping the site. NOAA CO-OPS tidesandcurrents is trivially usable (ACAO *, most permissive preflight in the cluster, 168-byte responses) but is water LEVEL only with no discharge product, so it is relevant to tidal-range questions, not river flow; note all its values are strings and its timestamp format "2026-08-11 01:36" needs T/Z normalization before new Date().

Elevation is orthometric (EGM2008) not ellipsoidal - correct default for head calculations. Slow relative to tiles: 8.8s for 256 points, so do NOT use this to build a dense profile; use it for a handful of anchor points.

notes:
DEFINITIVE RECOMMENDATION - HOW TO BUILD A RIVER-REACH ELEVATION PROFILE IN A BROWSER-ONLY APP

The single most important architectural point: a profile is O(reach length) if you use TILES and O(number of sample points) if you use a point API. Tiles win decisively. Once the ~3-20 tiles covering a reach are in memory you can sample 200 points or 5000 points for the same network cost - only cheap canvas reads differ. Every point API in this cluster caps at 100-256 points per request and would need 4-10 round trips for a dense profile.

PRIMARY: Re:Earth terrarium tiles.
  https://terrain.reearth.land/terrarium/elevation/{z}/{x}/{y}.png  (512x512, terrarium encoding, ACAO: *, Cache-Control 30 days, zoom to at least 17)
FALLBACK: AWS terrarium tiles.
  https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png  (256x256, ACAO: *, max zoom 15)
ANCHOR/CALIBRATION (US only): USGS EPQS, 2 requests (intake + powerhouse) for 1 m lidar truth + AcquisitionDate.
OPTIONAL DATUM CHECK: Re:Earth heights.json for the 2 endpoints, to get the geoid separation.

Decode in the browser: draw the PNG to an OffscreenCanvas, getImageData, then
  elev_m = (R * 256 + G + B / 256) - 32768
Both providers use identical terrarium encoding, so one decoder serves both. MapLibre can consume the same URLs directly as a raster-dem source with encoding:"terrarium" (tileSize 512 for Re:Earth, 256 with maxzoom 15 for AWS) - so the same tiles power 3D terrain, hillshade AND the profile chart with no extra downloads.

MEASURED VERTICAL ACCURACY (n=10 points, ground truth = USGS 3DEP 1 m EPQS, mix of Potomac lowland, Yellowstone 2516 m, Yosemite 1246 m):
  Re:Earth Mapterhorn    RMSE 0.91 m   max|err| 2.78 m   bias +0.25 m   <- best
  AWS terrarium z12      RMSE 2.30 m   max|err| 5.33 m   bias +0.43 m
  AWS terrarium z13      RMSE 2.45 m   max|err| 6.26 m   bias +0.86 m
  AWS terrarium z14      RMSE 2.47 m   max|err| 6.56 m   bias +1.01 m
  AWS terrarium z15      RMSE 2.54 m   max|err| 6.85 m   bias +1.13 m
  Open-Meteo GLO-90      RMSE 5.25 m   max|err| 8.94 m   bias +3.28 m
  Open-Elevation         RMSE 15.96 m  max|err| 44.02 m  bias +7.68 m   <- unusable
  USGS 3DEP EPQS         1 m grid, the reference itself
Note AWS RMSE barely changes with zoom - the error is in the DEM, not the sampling. Raising zoom buys spatial detail, not vertical accuracy. Independently, a spot check at 38.95,-77.12 gave AWS z15 = 79.066 m vs EPQS 3DEP = 79.033 m, a 0.03 m agreement, because the AWS source there is NED 1/9 arc-second lidar.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR GROSS HEAD (the error-sensitive input the task flagged): gross head is a DIFFERENCE of two elevations a few km apart, and DEM errors at nearby points are partly correlated, so the difference error is smaller than sqrt(2)*RMSE but not by much. Budget conservatively:
  Re:Earth Mapterhorn  ~ +/-1.3 m on head  -> ~1.3% power error on a 100 m head, ~0.13% on a 1000 m head
  AWS terrarium        ~ +/-3.5 m on head  -> ~3.5% on 100 m
  Open-Meteo GLO-90    ~ +/-7.4 m on head  -> ~7.4% on 100 m - marginal for a low-head site
  Open-Elevation       ~ +/-22 m on head   -> 22% on 100 m - disqualifying
For a low-head run-of-river scheme (head under ~20 m) even Mapterhorn's 1.3 m is 6-7% of head, so the UI must state that any sub-30 m head is a screening number requiring a real survey. For a high-head Himalayan scheme (500-1500 m gross head, as in the Trishuli/Budhi Gandaki probes) DEM error is under 0.3% and is not the limiting uncertainty - flow duration is.

REALISTIC POINT COUNTS AND TIMING (measured on a 14 km reach, 200 sample points, 6 parallel fetches):
  Re:Earth z12 (14.9 m ground sample):   3 tiles,  1.49 MB,  1.08 s
  Re:Earth z14 ( 3.7 m ground sample):  11 tiles,  4.59 MB,  2.71 s
  AWS      z13 (14.9 m ground sample):   6 tiles,  0.66 MB,  1.54 s
  AWS      z14 ( 7.4 m ground sample):  11 tiles,  1.11 MB,  3.02 s
  AWS      z15 ( 3.7 m ground sample):  21 tiles,  1.97 MB,  5.67 s
Gross drop computed from the same 200 points was stable to within 1.1 m across all AWS zooms (81.51 to 82.57 m), confirming z13 is enough for head. RECOMMENDED SETTING: Re:Earth z12-z13 (512 px) for reaches up to ~20 km. That is 3-6 tiles, 1.5-3 MB, roughly 1-2 s on a normal connection, and the 30-day Cache-Control makes a second reach in the same catchment effectively instant.
SAMPLE DENSITY: sample every 10-25 m along the channel polyline. For a 15 km reach that is 600-1500 points, and it costs ZERO extra network - the tiles are already in memory and canvas reads are microseconds. Do not ration sample points; ration tiles. A 200-point profile and a 1500-point profile have identical download cost.
LONGER REACHES: tile count grows roughly linearly with reach length. A 50 km reach at Re:Earth z12 is ~8-10 tiles / ~4-5 MB / ~2-3 s. Above ~100 km, drop to z11 for the overview and re-fetch at higher zoom only around the intake and powerhouse, where the head actually comes from.

MEASURED EFFECTIVE RESOLUTION (1 km transect sampled every 10 m, counting distinct values out of 100 - this is a much more honest test than the vendor's claimed resolution):
  Re:Earth heights.json  99/100 distinct  -> true fine-resolution DEM
  AWS terrarium z15      97/100 distinct  -> ~10 m effective here (NED 1/9 arc-sec source)
  Open-Meteo GLO-90       8/100 distinct, median plateau 9 samples -> ~90 m grid, matches the docs
  Open-Elevation          5/100 distinct, median plateau 23 samples -> ~230 m grid, i.e. SRTM 250 m
The Open-Elevation result is the important one: the public instance serves the AGGREGATED SRTM 250 m dataset, not SRTM 30 m as widely assumed.

CORRECTIONS TO DOCUMENTATION AND COMMON BELIEF
1. api.opentopodata.org does NOT support CORS. This is the headline correction. Numerous guides recommend it for browser apps. I verified ACAO is absent on 200 GETs with and without an Origin header, with a full Chrome header set including Sec-Fetch-*, on POST, and on 400 errors; and the OPTIONS preflight returns 204 with allow-methods and allow-headers but no ACAO, so preflight fails too. The project's own site confirms CORS is a paid GPXZ feature: "CORS (so you can use the API in your frontend webapp)". Public limits confirmed as documented: 100 locations/request, 1 call/sec, 1000 calls/day - and I tripped the per-second limit in normal sequential probing within seconds.
2. api.open-elevation.com is ALIVE and fast (5000 points via POST in 2.99 s, order preserved), contrary to its reputation for being down. It should nonetheless be rejected on accuracy (RMSE 16 m, max error 44 m, ~230 m grid), not liveness.
3. opentopodata datasets 3dep10m and srtm15plus do not exist ("Dataset not in config"). The US 10 m dataset is named ned10m.
4. AWS terrarium max zoom is 15, not 14 or 16. z16 returns 404.
5. EPQS moved to the /v1/json path; the older nationalmap.gov/epqs/pqs.php form is superseded. The current endpoint works and returns richer fields.

FREE FEATURES WORTH SHIPPING (fields already in responses we fetch anyway)
- x-amz-meta-x-imagery-sources on every AWS terrarium tile, CORS-EXPOSED via Access-Control-Expose-Headers so it is readable from fetch(). Observed values name the actual source raster: "ned/ned19_n39x00_w077x25_md_washingtondc_2008.tif", "srtm/N27E085.tif", "eudem/eudem_dem_5deg_n45e005.tif". Parse the prefix and you can label each reach with its true DEM and accuracy class ("this reach is backed by 2008 lidar, +/-1 m" vs "this reach is SRTM 30 m, +/-8 m") for free. Nothing else in this cluster offers per-reach provenance.
- Re:Earth heights.json returns geoid and ellipsoid alongside elevation (e.g. elevation 78.42, geoid -32.76, ellipsoid 45.66). This is the rarest useful field found. Hydropower survey data frequently arrives as GPS ellipsoidal heights; having the EGM2008 undulation at the exact site lets the app reconcile a surveyor's GPS number with the map elevation instead of silently comparing two different datums. It also declares the vertical datum explicitly, which no other free source in this cluster does.
- EPQS attributes.AcquisitionDate (observed: 11/3/2023, 11/3/2022, 6/6/2022, 9/3/2019) and resolution (1). Lets a US site show "elevation from 1 m lidar flown Nov 2023" - a credibility signal, free, in a response you already wanted.
- opentopodata results[].dataset names which DEM answered - useful, but unreachable from a browser.

COVERAGE GAPS AND TRAPS
- EPQS is US-only and fails ungracefully: HTTP 200, Content-Type: application/json, plain-text body. Two different failure strings observed at the same Nepal coordinate on different calls ("Call failed.  [Failed cloud operation: Open, Path: /vsimem/_00000B29.aux.xml]" and "Invalid or missing input parameters."). Any code doing res.json() on this throws. Guard with text() and a JSON sniff, and never gate on res.ok.
- EPQS type inconsistency: units=Meters returns value as a STRING, units=Feet returns it as a NUMBER. Always Number()-coerce.
- EPQS OPTIONS preflight returns 403. Keep the browser fetch a simple request - plain GET, zero custom headers. Adding an Accept or Content-Type header will break it in a browser even though curl succeeds.
- Re:Earth heights.json takes lon,lat order, the reverse of every other service here. This is the most likely silent bug in the whole cluster - a swapped pair in Nepal lands in the Indian Ocean and returns a plausible-looking negative number.
- Re:Earth is fronted by Cloudflare and 403s the default Python-urllib User-Agent. Browsers are unaffected; this only matters if the same URLs are ever probed from a script.
- AWS terrarium serves no Cache-Control (only ETag and Last-Modified 2017-11-12), so tiles may be re-downloaded on repeat visits. Re:Earth serves Cache-Control: public, max-age=2592000 and is much better behaved for a returning user. Consider caching decoded tiles in IndexedDB regardless.
- AWS terrarium data is frozen at 2017. Fine for terrain, but it will not reflect a reservoir built since.
- Terrarium encodes to 1/256 m = 0.0039 m precision. Do not let that leak into the UI - showing "79.066 m" implies 4 cm accuracy on data that is +/-2.5 m. Round displayed elevations to 1 m and displayed head to 1 m, and show the uncertainty band.
- All these DEMs are SURFACE-ish models over water: they give the water-surface elevation at the sampled date, not the bed. For a run-of-river profile that is actually what you want for gross head, but state it.
- Nepal/Himalaya specifically: AWS terrarium falls back to SRTM 30 m there (confirmed via the provenance header: srtm/N27E085.tif, srtm/N28E084.tif, srtm/N27E086.tif), so AWS accuracy in Nepal is materially worse than the US-derived RMSE of 2.5 m - expect SRTM-class ~6-10 m. Re:Earth Mapterhorn tracked AWS closely there (Trishuli 597.0 vs 599.4; Budhi Gandaki 1052.0 vs 1059.1; Kathmandu 1285.4 vs 1292.0) but no independent ground truth exists outside the US to score it, so do NOT claim sub-metre accuracy outside the US. Present accuracy as source-dependent, driven by the provenance header.

HTTPS worked on every endpoint probed. No endpoint required a key except MapTiler. Nothing needed a proxy except opentopodata, which needs one absolutely.

notes:
DEFINITIVE ANSWER TO THE PRACTICAL QUESTION — "can a static browser app get upstream catchment area at a point on a river, with no backend, no key, no proxy?"

**YES for North and South America, today, with zero preprocessing. NO for the rest of the world as a live API — but YES globally with a one-time offline build step.** Three separate findings, in order of practical value:

**(1) The Americas are solved outright.** Esri's Living Atlas hosts HydroSHEDS 2.0 River Streamlines as a public, authoritative, key-free ArcGIS FeatureServer with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. A single simple GET (no preflight) returns UPLAND_SKM directly. VALIDATED AGAINST GROUND TRUTH: querying 38.95,-77.12 (Potomac at Little Falls) returned UPLAND_SKM = 30,003.39 km2; the USGS published drainage area at Little Falls is 11,560 sq mi = 29,940 km2 — a 0.2% match. Wire cost was 845 bytes brotli for 6 reaches WITH geometry. This is a one-fetch feature.

**(2) There is no global equivalent, and I looked hard.** I enumerated every candidate: ArcGIS Online has ~74 HydroRIVERS items and ~401 HydroSHEDS items, but every global-attribute one is a small regional clip by an individual user (Namibia lon 16.9-23.1; West Africa lon -17.0 to -4.9; Central Asia lon 42.8-87.6). Google Earth Engine has HydroATLAS globally but returns `HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` — OAuth-only, disqualified. No PMTiles, vector-tile, GeoParquet or FlatGeobuf build of HydroRIVERS/HydroBASINS/RiverATLAS exists on any CORS-enabled CDN (checked source.coop, AWS Open Data, jsDelivr, GitHub). The only global sources are bulk file downloads.

**(3) The global build path is wide open, because the official host is fully CORS-enabled including Range.** data.hydrosheds.org returns `access-control-allow-origin: <your-origin>` on GET, on ranged GET (206 with `content-range: bytes 100-200/9377170`), and on OPTIONS preflight — and explicitly answers `access-control-allow-headers: range`. Combined with `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, this means a cloud-optimized format hosted there WOULD be range-readable from a browser. It just isn't offered in one. So: download HydroRIVERS per continent offline, convert to PMTiles or FlatGeobuf, host on GitHub Pages / Cloudflare R2 (both `ACAO: *` + 206 verified), done. Still no backend.

**Runtime fetch of the raw files is NOT viable — with numbers.** Smallest useful continent is North America at 66,335,898 B (63.3 MB) or Europe at 67,648,957 B (64.5 MB); Africa is 107,873,468 B (102.9 MB); global is 544,388,154 B (519.2 MB). Beyond the transfer cost, the .sbn/.sbx spatial index is ESRI-proprietary and undocumented, so JS cannot use it — a browser would have to linearly parse the entire .shp. Verdict: preprocess, don't stream.

**THE HEADLINE FREE FEATURE — no RiverATLAS download required.** The single highest-value finding: base HydroRIVERS v1.0 ALREADY carries both upstream area and long-term discharge. You do NOT need the 2.25 GB RiverATLAS file for the core hydropower calculation. I parsed the actual DBF (137,088 records, 14 fields, 103-byte records) out of the 9.38 MB Greenland tile and confirmed on a real record (HYRIV_ID 90007489): UPLAND_SKM = 76522.2 and DIS_AV_CMS = 141.413. Fourteen fields total, including NEXT_DOWN for full network traversal, ORD_CLAS (=1 identifies main-stem "backbone" rivers for free), and HYBAS_L12 to join catchment polygons. RiverATLAS adds 281 more attributes on top of these same reaches, joined on HYRIV_ID — so you can ship base HydroRIVERS first and layer RiverATLAS in later without re-architecting.

**UNITS — CONFIRMED FROM LIVE DATA, AND THIS IS A REAL TRAP.** The prompt correctly flagged that USGS reports discharge in cubic FEET per second. HydroSHEDS does NOT. DIS_AV_CMS is CUBIC METERS PER SECOND — confirmed three ways: the field name suffix, the live value 141.413 on a Greenland reach, and the HydroRIVERS TechDoc verbatim ("Average long-term discharge estimate for river reach, in cubic meters per second"). RiverATLAS `dis_m3_pyr` returned exactly the same value as `DIS_AV_CMS` (both 3.059 at a Kyrgyz reach), confirming they are the same quantity. Areas are SQUARE KILOMETERS throughout (USGS StreamStats uses square miles). Mixing a USGS cfs/sq-mi feed with a HydroSHEDS m3/s/km2 feed in the same app without conversion would produce errors of 35x on flow and 2.6x on area.

**FURTHER UNIT TRAP INSIDE HydroATLAS.** Several RiverATLAS columns are stored as integer FACTORS of the nominal unit to save space — the TechDoc states temperature is in tenths of a degree, and `sgr_dk_rav` is in DECIMETERS per km (observed value 44 = 4.4 m/km). `slp_dg_uav` returned 211, which is degrees scaled by a factor, not 211 degrees. The per-variable factor is documented ONLY in the 65.6 MB RiverATLAS_Catalog_v10.pdf. Verify every column you use; do not assume SI.

**HIGHEST-VALUE RiverATLAS COLUMNS FOR HYDROPOWER**, with real observed values at a Kyrgyz reach (HYRIV_ID 40258625): `dis_m3_pmn` = 0.321 m3/s — the long-term MINIMUM-month discharge, which is the firm-power number that actually determines a run-of-river plant's guaranteed output, and it is not in base HydroRIVERS; `dis_m3_pmx` = 11.402 m3/s (max month, a 35x seasonal swing); `sgr_dk_rav` = 44 dm/km = 4.4 m of head per km of channel — head and flow together are literally the hydropower equation; `ele_mt_cav`=668 / `ele_mt_uav`=2577 m.a.s.l. giving 1,909 m of upstream relief; `dor_pc_pva` = 0% degree of regulation, i.e. whether upstream dams already exist; `gla_pc_use` and `snw_pc_uyr`=40% for melt-driven seasonality. The full 297-field schema is enumerated in the RiverATLAS source entry.

**CORRECTIONS TO PUBLISHED/ASSUMED DOCUMENTATION:**
- HydroATLAS data is NOT on data.hydrosheds.org. All four plausible paths under /file/hydroatlas/ return `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found, Content-Length: 94`. Only the TechDoc and Catalog PDFs live there; the DATA is on figshare article 9890531. Corrected URLs are in the figshare entry.
- api.figshare.com is a CORS FALSE FRIEND. It returns Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, -Allow-Methods, -Allow-Headers and -Expose-Headers but NO Access-Control-Allow-Origin — verified with an Origin, without an Origin, and on an OPTIONS preflight. Browsers will block it. Meanwhile the file host (ndownloader.figshare.com) IS correctly CORS-enabled with Range support and readable Content-Range. You can download from a browser but you cannot list; hard-code the file IDs.
- The Esri Basins layer's advertised `extent` metadata is WRONG (reports a ~0.4-degree box in Brazil for a 21.45M-feature Americas-wide layer). Never trust ArcGIS extent metadata for coverage; probe with actual point queries, which is how I established the Americas-only boundary.
- Use `ndownloader.figshare.com/files/<id>` not `figshare.com/ndownloader/files/<id>` — the latter returns an `HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted, Content-Length: 0` AWS WAF interstitial.

**SEMANTIC TRAP THAT WOULD SILENTLY PRODUCE WRONG ANSWERS.** Do not use point-in-polygon on the Esri Basins layer to get upstream area, despite UPLAND_SKM being right there and the alias reading "Upland Area (sq km)". Those are 21.45M ELEMENTARY catchments; a click at the Potomac returns UPLAND_SKM = 12.567 km2 because the point landed on a small hillslope catchment beside the river, not the main stem — a 2,400x underestimate versus the correct 30,003 km2. I confirmed the field really is accumulated (not local) via a stats query: WHERE MAIN_BAS=84862 gives max=35,034.84 km2 over n=18,733 catchments with sum=9,298,699 km2, a sum far exceeding the basin's true area, which only makes sense for nested accumulated values. The correct pattern is always: SNAP TO THE STREAMLINES LAYER, then read UPLAND_SKM.

**COVERAGE GAPS — the honest picture.** Per the instruction to probe both US and non-US points, I tested Potomac (38.95,-77.12), Nepal/Kathmandu (27.7,85.3), Switzerland (47.5,8.5), Rhine (49.0,8.3), Amazon/Manaus (-3.1,-60.0), Mississippi/St. Louis (38.6,-90.2), Willamette/Portland (45.6,-122.3) and Kyrgyzstan (42.9,74.6). Result: the only key-free live API (Esri) covers the Americas and returns literally zero features for Nepal and Switzerland on all seven Strahler layers. Given this project's directory name suggests open-source hydropower — and that Nepal is one of the world's most hydropower-relevant countries — this gap is the central constraint. Nepal is served ONLY by the bulk-download-plus-preprocess path: HydroRIVERS_v10_as_shp.zip at 90,510,995 B (86.3 MB), which is entirely tractable as an offline build input.

**RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE.** Two tiers. Tier 1 (ship this week): Esri HydroSHEDS 2.0 Streamlines for the Americas, one fetch, zero build, sub-kilobyte responses. Tier 2 (global): offline-convert HydroRIVERS per continent to PMTiles or FlatGeobuf keeping just HYRIV_ID, UPLAND_SKM, DIS_AV_CMS, NEXT_DOWN, ORD_STRA, then optionally left-join RiverATLAS's dis_m3_pmn and sgr_dk_rav on HYRIV_ID; host on GitHub Pages or Cloudflare R2 and range-read from the browser. Both tiers are genuinely backend-free. Size estimate for tier 2: the Greenland DBF is 14,120,546 B raw / 2,944,238 B deflated for 137,088 reaches, so a global attributes-only table for ~8.5M reaches scales to roughly 180 MB deflated in DBF terms — and far less in a columnar format retaining only the five fields above.

**RATE LIMITS — the one real operational risk.** The Esri service exposes its budget in response headers, observed verbatim: `x-esri-query-request-units: 2` per spatial query and `x-esri-org-request-units-per-min: usage=625;max=57600`. That is roughly 28,800 queries/minute, but it is a quota belonging to Esri's org and SHARED with every other consumer of that Living Atlas layer — you neither control nor can raise it. A burst of 25 rapid requests all returned 200 with no 429 and no Retry-After. Cache aggressively client-side; the underlying data is static. By contrast data.hydrosheds.org showed no rate limiting of any kind and served the 9.38 MB Greenland tile in 0.54 s. HTTPS works everywhere; data.hydrosheds.org enforces HSTS (max-age=63072000) behind Cloudflare + Backblaze B2.

**Performance caveat worth designing around.** The Esri low-Strahler-order layers (L4/L5/L6, up to 4.9M features) are slow — several point+distance queries against them exceeded 30 s and timed out during probing. Use a tight `esriGeometryEnvelope` rather than point+distance on those layers, and query high-order layers first since a user clicking a "river" usually means a visible one.

**Licensing is clean for commercial use.** HydroSHEDS/HydroRIVERS/HydroBASINS are free for scientific, educational AND commercial use with attribution. HydroATLAS is CC-BY 4.0 as a collective database (individual columns CC-BY 4.0 or ODbL 1.0), DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.9890531.v1 — both licenses explicitly permit commercial reuse. The Esri Living Atlas item is public/authoritative with licenseInfo attached; check its terms before commercial redistribution of derived values.

**Method note on one instruction.** The task suggested `curl -sI` as acceptable for reading content-length. I used ranged GETs (`-r 0-0`) and full header dumps (`-s -D - -o /dev/null`) throughout instead, consistent with the methodology section's warning that many APIs reject HEAD. This proved to be the right call: it simultaneously measured file sizes AND proved 206/Range support, which is the load-bearing fact for any future cloud-optimized-format strategy on this host. Two objects (hybas_af_lev01-12 and HydroLAKES_polys) returned 200 instead of 206 to a range request, so their sizes came from a plain GET header dump; HydroRIVERS_v10.gdb.zip and the global shp were slow enough that the first attempt timed out and I re-probed with ranged requests.
