notes:
VERDICT: Overpass is fully usable from a browser-only static app — no key, no proxy, no backend. Every live instance sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and POST preflight is explicitly verified working (`Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type`, `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600`). The blocker is not CORS, it is availability.

=== BIGGEST PRACTICAL WIN: SKIP THE PREFLIGHT ===
Instead of `data=<query>` form-encoded, POST the raw Overpass QL as the request body with `Content-Type: text/plain`. text/plain is a CORS-safelisted content type, so the browser sends NO preflight at all — one round trip instead of two. Verified working: HTTP/1.1 200 OK, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, `Content-Encoding: gzip`, `Content-Type: application/json`. This is the pattern to ship.

=== CORRECTION #1: `waterway=penstock` DOES NOT EXIST (this was in the task brief) ===
`nwr["waterway"="penstock"]` over ALL of Switzerland (45.8,5.9,47.8,10.5) returns `{"nodes":"0","ways":"0","relations":"0","total":"0"}`. Zero. The real tagging is:
  - `man_made=pipeline` + `usage=penstock` -> 725 ways in CH
  - `usage=penstock` (any element) -> 733 in CH, 7 in all Nepal, 8 in the whole US Pacific NW
  - `usage~"headrace|tailrace"` -> 865 in CH, 5 in all Nepal
  - `man_made=pipeline` + `substance=water` -> 1,550 in CH (broader, includes non-hydro)
Use `usage=penstock`, never `waterway=penstock`.

=== CORRECTION #2: kumi.systems IS private.coffee ===
DNS: `overpass.kumi.systems` and `overpass.private.coffee` are both aliases of `flanders.servers.private.coffee` / 193.219.97.30, confirmed by the `PC-Overpass-Worker` response header appearing on kumi requests. Listing them as two failover targets is useless. Worse, that host serves STALE AND NON-DETERMINISTIC data: sampling `osm3s.timestamp_osm_base` across repeated identical calls returned 2026-05-06, 2026-05-31, and 2026-06-24 depending on which worker answered (real date 2026-08-11) — 6 to 14 weeks behind, and two identical queries can disagree. It also serves NO compression (21,007 B vs 3,059 B gzipped elsewhere, ~7x bandwidth).

=== CORRECTION #3: three widely-cited mirrors are dead ===
overpass.osm.jp — TLS cert EXPIRED (`SEC_E_CERT_EXPIRED`); browsers hard-fail. overpass.nchc.org.tw, overpass.osm.ru — no DNS record. overpass.openstreetmap.ru — connection timeout.

=== THE REAL RISK: RELIABILITY, NOT CORS ===
overpass-api.de enforces 2 concurrent slots per IP (`/api/status`: "Rate limit: 2"). Measured on an identical realistic 30km viewport query: 43% success at 6s spacing, and still only 50% success (4/8) at 20s spacing — failures split between HTTP 429 (`...::rate_limited`) and HTTP 504 (`...::timeout. The server is probably too busy`). Mitigating factors: the quota is charged to the END USER's IP (not the app), so one user panning a map is far lighter than my test. Still, a mirror-failover chain is mandatory. Recommended order, all CORS-verified: (1) overpass-api.de, (2) maps.mail.ru/osm/tools/overpass — the only other mirror with SAME-DAY data, gzip, and no observed rate limit, though it is a VK/Mail.ru endpoint so there is a jurisdiction/availability judgement call, (3) overpass.monicz.dev — zstd-compressed but ~5 weeks stale, (4) lz4/z.overpass-api.de as intra-cluster retries (note: these SHARE the main quota, same "Connected as: 3392360666" identity — round-robinning them does not buy extra requests), (5) private.coffee/kumi as last resort with a staleness warning in the UI.

=== TWO SILENT-FAILURE TRAPS ===
1. A server-side query timeout returns **HTTP 200** with an empty `elements` array and a top-level `"remark"` field: `"remark": "runtime error: Query timed out in \"query\" at line 1 after 4 seconds."` HTTP 200 does NOT mean complete data — the app must check `remark` on every response or it will silently render an empty map.
2. Errors (429/504) are returned as **XHTML, not JSON**, so `JSON.parse()` throws. Check `response.status` and content-type before parsing.

=== GET vs POST LENGTH LIMIT (measured) ===
Encoded URL 4,175 chars -> 200. Encoded URL 8,255 chars -> **HTTP 414 Request-URI Too Long** (Apache LimitRequestLine, 8190). The same 7,486-char query via POST -> 200. Multi-tag hydro queries cross 8 KB fast, so POST is the safe default.

=== PAYLOAD SIZES ARE TINY — PRELOADING IS VIABLE ===
Full 30km Alpine viewport (dams+weirs+plants+generators+penstocks, `out center tags`): 20,761 B raw / **3,059 B gzipped**, 77 elements, 2-5s warm. `out center tags` vs `out geom` on the same features: 8,334 B raw / 1,782 B gzip vs 37,478 B raw / 7,338 B gzip — geometry costs ~4x, so use `out center tags` for markers and only fetch `out geom` on click. Whole-country preloads are practical: ALL 138 Nepal hydro plants+generators = 6,200 B gzipped; all 1,299 Swiss ones = 69,813 B gzipped. Nepal's entire hydro fleet fits in one 6 KB fetch.

=== `out:csv` IS A HUGE BANDWIDTH WIN AND IS UNDER-USED ===
`[out:csv(::type,::id,::lat,::lon,name,"plant:output:electricity",operator,"plant:method";true;"|")]` with `out center` returns a clean pipe-delimited table WITH the computed centroid already filled in for ways and relations. Real output: `way|101843835|46.2832825|7.6886943|Turtmann|8.2 MW|Argessa AG|water-pumped-storage`. Roughly 5x smaller than JSON when you only need a fixed column set.

=== OSM COVERAGE PER REGION — THE HONEST ANSWER ===
Point presence is decent everywhere; ATTRIBUTE quality is wildly regional. Share of hydro plants/generators carrying each tag:
- Switzerland (n=1299): name 63%, capacity present 90%, capacity NUMERIC 64%, operator 61%, method 72%, start_date 31%, wikidata 17%
- US Pacific NW (n=234): name 57%, capacity present 88%, capacity NUMERIC 57%, operator 53%, method 24%, start_date 44%, wikidata 26%
- Nepal (n=138): name 58%, capacity present 53%, capacity NUMERIC only 35%, operator 13%, method 38%, start_date 2%, wikidata 3%
The Nepal Marsyangdi hydro corridor — a genuinely dam-dense valley — returned 8 features of which 6 dams and 1 weir carried the single tag `{"waterway":"dam"}` with NO name, height, operator or capacity whatsoever. Plan the UI for null attributes outside Europe/North America; do not build a card layout that assumes capacity and operator exist.

=== DATA-QUALITY GOTCHAS IN THE TAGS THEMSELVES ===
- `plant:output:electricity` / `generator:output:electricity` are FREE-TEXT strings with embedded units: real values seen include "1162 MW", "8.2 MW", "45 MW" — but also the useless literal "yes" (that is why "capacity present" is 90% in CH while "capacity NUMERIC" is only 64%). Parse defensively and handle MW/kW/GW suffixes.
- `height` is a bare number in METRES with no unit tag: "148" for Barrage de Moiry, "156" for a reinforced-concrete dam relation, "33", "49.5".
- `year_of_construction` has dirty values with trailing periods: "1958.", "1923.", "1927.". `start_date` is cleaner ("1969", "1938-07"). Check both keys.
- Ways and relations have NO lat/lon — you must request `out center` to get `center:{lat,lon}`, otherwise you get geometry-less elements you cannot place on a map.

=== FREE CROSS-DATASET JOIN KEYS (the most valuable find) ===
Fields already present in responses you would fetch anyway, enabling joins to other sources at zero extra cost:
- `ref:US:NID` = "VA059001" — US Army Corps National Inventory of Dams ID (on Lake Barcroft Dam, node/356577449)
- `ref:US:EIA` = "3075" — EIA plant code (on Bonneville Powerhouses, relation/6287521, `plant:output:electricity` "1162 MW", `start_date` "1938-07")
- `gnis:feature_id` = "1489655" — USGS GNIS feature ID, joins to the USGS gazetteer
- `wikidata` = "Q26265740" / `wikipedia` / `wikimedia_commons` — free article links and photos
- `source` provenance strings, e.g. "U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA-860 - 2020" and "Office fédéral de l'énergie - Statistique des aménagements hydroélectriques - 2020"
- `osm3s.timestamp_osm_base` in every response = free freshness indicator AND the only way to detect a stale mirror
- `osm3s.copyright` = the ODbL attribution string, returned automatically (attribution IS required — data is ODbL)
Also present: `name:en` / `name:ne` / `name:new` for localized labels, `ele`, `material`, `location` ("underground"), `plant:method` ("run-of-the-river" / "water-storage" / "water-pumped-storage"), `operator:wikidata`, and `disused` (16 occurrences in the Alpine box — filter these out or the map will show decommissioned plants as live).

MINOR: HEAD requests are unanswered, as the brief warned — all probing used real GETs/POSTs with `-D -`. Plain `http://` also returns 200 with ACAO: * (no forced HTTPS redirect), but HTTPS works everywhere and should be used. maps.mail.ru rejects queries that omit an explicit `[timeout:N]`, so always include one.

topic: Independent physics validation baseline for a run-of-river hydropower prefeasibility calculator (power equation, FDC energy integration, real-plant back-calculations, unit constants, plausible ranges)
evidence:
========================================================================
1. THE POWER EQUATION — CONSTANTS, UNITS, WORKED BY HAND
========================================================================

P = rho * g * Q * H * eta

  rho  [kg/m^3]  water density
  g    [m/s^2]   gravitational acceleration
  Q    [m^3/s]   flow through the turbine
  H    [m]       NET head (gross head minus hydraulic losses)
  eta  [-]       overall efficiency (dimensionless, 0..1)
  P    [W]       = kg/m^3 * m/s^2 * m^3/s * m = kg*m^2/s^3 = W   (units check OK)

CONSTANTS (values verified against standards, not guessed):
  g = 9.80665 m/s^2 exactly  (standard gravity, CGPM 3rd conf. 1901 / SI Brochure)
      Local g ranges 9.7803 (equator) to 9.8322 (poles) = +/-0.27%.
  rho fresh water at 1 atm (IAPWS-95):
      0  C : 999.8395 kg/m^3
      4  C : 999.9720 kg/m^3   (max density)
      10 C : 999.7026 kg/m^3   <-- the value asked for
      15 C : 999.1026 kg/m^3
      20 C : 998.2071 kg/m^3
  Engineering practice (ESHA 2004 Layman's Guidebook, sec. 3.5) uses
      gamma = rho*g = 9.81 kN/m^3, i.e. rho = 1000, g = 9.81.

  Specific-weight products (N/m^3), computed:
      1000   * 9.81     = 9810.000000
      1000   * 9.80665  = 9806.650000
      999.7026 * 9.80665 = 9803.7335
      999.7026 * 9.81     = 9807.0825

RECOMMENDATION FOR THE TOOL: hard-code rho = 1000.0 kg/m^3 and g = 9.81 m/s^2
(matches ESHA/industry). The maximum spread against the "physically exact 10 C"
pair (999.7026 / 9.80665) is only 0.064%, so cross-convention asserts should
use a tolerance of +/-0.1%, NOT bit equality.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
WORKED EXAMPLE BY HAND: Q = 10 m^3/s, H = 50 m, eta = 0.85
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Using rho = 1000, g = 9.81:

  step 1  rho * g          = 1000 * 9.81            =      9,810      N/m^3
  step 2  (rho*g) * Q      = 9,810 * 10             =     98,100      N/s   (= 98.1 kN/s)
  step 3  (rho*g*Q) * H    = 98,100 * 50            =  4,905,000      W     (hydraulic power)
                                                    =  4,905.000      kW
                                                    =  4.905000       MW
  step 4  * eta            = 4,905,000 * 0.85       =  4,169,250      W     <-- ANSWER

  P = 4,169,250 W
    = 4,169,250 / 1000        = 4,169.25    kW
    = 4,169,250 / 1,000,000   = 4.16925     MW

  (0.85 * 4,905,000: 4,905,000 - 0.15*4,905,000 = 4,905,000 - 735,750 = 4,169,250. Checks.)

ALTERNATIVE CONSTANT SETS (assert-ready, exact decimal arithmetic):
  rho=1000,     g=9.81     -> P = 4,169,250.0000        W = 4.16925000000000  MW
  rho=1000,     g=9.80665  -> P = 4,167,826.2500        W = 4.16782625000000  MW  (-0.0341%)
  rho=999.7,    g=9.80665  -> P = 4,166,575.9021250     W = 4.16657590212500  MW  (-0.0641%)
  rho=999.7,    g=9.81     -> P = 4,167,999.2250        W = 4.16799922500000  MW  (-0.0300%)
  rho=998.2071, g=9.80665  -> P = 4,160,324.1626        W = 4.16032416260000  MW  (-0.2141%)

========================================================================
2. ANNUAL ENERGY, AND CAPACITY FACTOR vs PLANT FACTOR
========================================================================

E = P * 8760 h   (constant-power idealisation only)

  P = 4,169,250 W = 4,169.25 kW = 4.16925 MW
  E = 4,169.25 kW * 8760 h = 36,522,630        kWh
                            = 36,522.63         MWh   (kWh / 1e3)
                            = 36.52263          GWh   (kWh / 1e6, or MWh / 1e3)
  Cross-check: 4.16925 MW * 8760 h = 36,522.63 MWh. Same number. OK.

  With g = 9.80665, rho = 1000  : E = 36.510157950  GWh
  With g = 9.80665, rho = 999.7 : E = 36.499204903  GWh

CRITICAL: 36.52 GWh is the 100%-capacity-factor ceiling. It is NOT a
prefeasibility answer. It presumes 10 m^3/s is available 8760 h/yr with zero
outages. A real ROR plant at PF 0.55 yields ~20.1 GWh. Any tool that reports
"P * 8760" as annual energy is wrong by roughly a factor of 2.

HOURS-PER-YEAR CONSTANTS:
  8760 h = 365 d      (standard, use this)
  8766 h = 365.25 d   (mean Julian year; +0.0685% vs 8760)
  8784 h = 366 d      (leap year; +0.274% vs 8760)

------------------------------------------------------------------------
CAPACITY FACTOR vs PLANT FACTOR — PRECISE DEFINITIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------------
CAPACITY FACTOR (CF):
  CF = E_actual [MWh over period] / (P_nameplate [MW] * hours in period)
  Denominator uses INSTALLED / NAMEPLATE capacity. It is a measured,
  ex-post quantity: it embeds hydrology AND forced outages AND planned
  maintenance AND grid curtailment AND (depending on metering point)
  transformer and auxiliary losses.

PLANT FACTOR (= LOAD FACTOR in European/ESHA usage):
  ESHA 2004 glossary, verbatim: "Load factor: Is defined as the ratio
  annual energy output kWh/max power output x 8760 hours".
  Denominator uses the plant's MAXIMUM ACHIEVABLE power output. When
  max achievable output == nameplate, plant factor and capacity factor
  are numerically identical; they diverge when the plant is derated
  (worn runners, head loss, restricted tailwater, unit out of service).

WHICH ONE DOES AN FDC INTEGRATION PRODUCE?
  An FDC integration produces a GROSS/THEORETICAL PLANT FACTOR, not a
  capacity factor. The FDC contains hydrology only. It contains no
  outage data, no availability, no curtailment, no station service load.
  Therefore:

      PF_fdc  =  E_fdc / (P_rated * 8760)
      CF_real =  PF_fdc * A * (1 - aux) * (1 - curtail)
                 where A = availability, typically 0.90-0.97 for hydro

  ASSERT: CF_reported <= PF_fdc always. If your tool computes E from an FDC
  and then calls the result a "capacity factor", it is overstating output by
  the availability factor (3-10%). Label it "gross plant factor" and apply an
  explicit availability multiplier to get a bankable capacity factor.

========================================================================
3. CORRECT ANNUAL ENERGY FROM A FLOW-DURATION CURVE
========================================================================

Let D in [0,1] be EXCEEDANCE PROBABILITY (fraction of time flow is equalled
or exceeded). Q(D) is the natural river flow; Q(D) is MONOTONE DECREASING
(Q(0) = flood peak, Q(1) = absolute minimum flow).

ORDER OF OPERATIONS (this order is not negotiable):

  (a) SUBTRACT RESIDUAL FLOW FIRST, from the natural river flow:
          Q_avail(D) = max(0, Q(D) - Q_res)
      Q_res is compensation/reserved/environmental flow. It is bypassed at
      the intake and is unavailable to the turbine at ALL times, including
      drought. Subtracting it after the design-flow cap is a common and
      material bug (it silently gives the plant free water in the dry season).

  (b) CAP AT DESIGN FLOW (turbine swallowing capacity):
          Q_cap(D) = min(Q_avail(D), Q_d)
      Excess spills over the weir and produces zero energy.

  (c) APPLY MINIMUM TECHNICAL FLOW (cut-out):
          Q_t(D) = Q_cap(D)   if Q_cap(D) >= Q_min
                 = 0          if Q_cap(D) <  Q_min
      Q_min = f_min * Q_d. This is a HARD DISCONTINUITY, not a taper.

  (d) POWER AT EACH EXCEEDANCE:
          P(D) = rho * g * H_n(Q_t) * Q_t(D) * eta(Q_t / Q_d)
      eta is a FUNCTION of part-load ratio, not a constant. H_n also varies
      with flow in low-head schemes (tailwater rise).

  (e) INTEGRATE OVER EXCEEDANCE PROBABILITY:

          E  =  T * INTEGRAL_{D=0}^{D=1} P(D) dD ,    T = 8760 h

      Units: P in kW, D dimensionless, T in h  ->  E in kWh.
      Note dD, NOT dQ. Integrating over discharge is the single most common
      conceptual error and gives a meaningless answer.

  SANITY IDENTITY (assert this): sum of all strip widths must equal exactly
  1.0 (or 100%). If your quadrature weights do not sum to 1, E is scaled wrong.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
TRAPEZOIDAL-RULE DETAIL ON THE 0-100% EXCEEDANCE AXIS
------------------------------------------------------------------------
With samples D_0 = 0 < D_1 < ... < D_N = 1 and P_i = P(D_i):

    E = T * SUM_{i=0}^{N-1} 0.5 * (P_i + P_{i+1}) * (D_{i+1} - D_i)

Rules that must hold:
  * BOTH ENDPOINTS MUST EXIST. D = 0 and D = 1 must be sample points. A
    common bug is sampling D = 5%,10%,...,95%, which covers only 0.90 of the
    probability mass (or 0.95 with half-strips) and biases E low by ~5-10%.
    If the raw FDC starts at Q5 and ends at Q95, you must extrapolate or
    explicitly document the truncation.
  * INSERT A NODE AT EVERY BREAKPOINT. The integrand P(D) is piecewise
    smooth with two kinks and one jump:
       D_cap  where Q(D) = Q_res + Q_d     (P becomes flat/constant to the left)
       D_cut  where Q(D) = Q_res + Q_min   (P JUMPS to 0 to the right)
    A trapezoid straddling D_cut linearly smears a step discontinuity and
    over-credits energy in the dry tail. Solve for D_cap and D_cut by
    inverting the FDC and add them as explicit nodes, with P evaluated at
    D_cut^- = rho*g*H*Q_min*eta(f_min) and at D_cut^+ = 0.
  * LEFT-TAIL CURVATURE IS HARMLESS AFTER CAPPING. Raw FDCs are near-vertical
    at D -> 0, where the trapezoid rule performs badly. But the Q_d cap makes
    P(D) exactly constant on [0, D_cap], so the trapezoid is EXACT there.
    The remaining error concentrates in the steep dry tail — refine there.
  * FDC ON A LOG-Q AXIS: never trapezoid in log space and exponentiate;
    integrate P linearly in D.

ESHA'S OWN METHOD (for cross-validation, Layman's Guidebook sec. 3.5, verbatim):
  "It divides the useable area into vertical 5% incremental strips starting
   from the origin. The final strip will intersect the FDC at Qmin or
   Qreserved which ever is larger. For each strip Qmedian is calculated ...
   and the energy contribution of the strip is calculated using the equation:
      DE = W.Qmedian.H.hturbine.hgenerator.hgearbox.htransformer.g.h
   where W = strip width = 0.05 for all strips except the last one that
   should be calculated, h = number of hours in a year, g = specific weight
   of the water (9.81 KNm-3)"
  Note: this is a MIDPOINT (rectangle) rule on 5% strips, not a trapezoid.
  Midpoint and trapezoid bracket the truth for a convex FDC — a good
  regression test is that the two agree within ~1-2% at 5% strips and
  converge as strips shrink.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
DESIGN-FLOW SELECTION (ESHA, verbatim, sec. 3.5)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
  "Usually the design flow is assumed to be, in a first approach, the
   difference between the mean annual flow and the reserved flow. In actual
   practice is strongly recommended to evaluate the plant for other design
   flows in order to choose, the one that yields the best results."
  i.e. Q_d,first-pass = Q_mean - Q_res, then sweep Q_d.

========================================================================
4. THREE REAL PUBLISHED RUN-OF-RIVER PLANTS — BACK-CALCULATED
========================================================================
Back-calc definitions used:
  eta_implied = P_installed / (rho * g * Q_design * H)      with rho=1000, g=9.81
  PF_implied  = E_annual / (P_installed * 8760 h)

--- PLANT A: Kaligandaki 'A', Nepal (ROR with daily pondage, 3x Francis) ---
  Installed        144 MW
  Rated discharge  141 m^3/s (total)
  Net head         115 m   (gross head 130 m)
  Annual energy    842 GWh/yr (NEA design value; Wikipedia lists 860 GWh)
  Commissioned     2002
  Hydraulic power  1000*9.81*141*115       = 159,069,150 W = 159.07 MW
  eta_implied      144 / 159.07            = 0.9053
  PF_implied       842e3 MWh /(144*8760)   = 0.6675   (0.6818 if 860 GWh)
  COMMENT: eta 0.905 is at the top of but inside the credible band for a
  large Francis + synchronous generator (0.94 * 0.97 = 0.912). Sources
  disagree on discharge (one lists 44.86 m^3/s per unit -> 134.58 total,
  which would imply eta 0.9485 — physically implausible; the 141 m^3/s
  total figure is the self-consistent one). Using GROSS head 130 m instead
  of net 115 m gives eta 0.8008 — a clean demonstration of the gross/net
  head trap (14.3% error).
  Sources:
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaligandaki_A_Hydroelectric_Power_Station
    https://nwrmap.pei.center/hydropower/kaligandaki-a-hydropower-station
    https://www.adb.org/features/kali-gandaki-hydroelectric-project-report-card
    https://www.hydropower.org/sediment-management-case-studies/nepal-kali-gandaki

--- PLANT B: Upper Tamakoshi, Nepal (peaking ROR, 6x Pelton) ---
  Installed        456 MW  (6 x 76.5 MW / 90 MVA)
  Design discharge 66 m^3/s
  Head             822 m gross, 805 m rated (Andritz, verbatim)
  Annual energy    2,281 GWh/yr (design)
  Full commercial operation 2021
  Hydraulic power (rated H)  1000*9.81*66*805 = 521.21 MW
  eta_implied (rated H 805)  456 / 521.21     = 0.8749
  eta_implied (gross H 822)  456 / 532.21     = 0.8568
  PF_implied                 2281e3/(456*8760)= 0.5710
  COMMENT: eta 0.875 is textbook for multi-jet Pelton (0.90) x generator
  (0.97) = 0.873. Excellent agreement — this is the best single validation
  point in the set.
  Sources:
    https://www.andritz.com/hydro-en/hydronews/26/hy-news-26-19-upper-tamakoshi-hydro
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Tamakoshi_Hydroelectric_Project
    https://www.power-technology.com/projects/upper-tamakoshi-hydroelectric-project/
    https://norconsult.com/projects/upper-tamakoshi-hydroelectric-project/

--- PLANT C: Rheinfelden, Germany/Switzerland (low-head ROR, 4x Kaplan bulb) ---
  Installed        100 MW
  Design discharge 1500 m^3/s
  Head             8.5 m ("Average head", Fichtner, verbatim)
  Annual energy    600 GWh/yr average (up from 185 GWh at the old plant)
  Commissioned     2010
  Hydraulic power  1000*9.81*1500*8.5 = 125.08 MW
  eta_implied      100 / 125.08       = 0.7995
  PF_implied       600e3/(100*8760)   = 0.6849
  COMMENT: 0.80 is BELOW what a modern Kaplan bulb achieves (~0.93 * 0.97
  = 0.90). The discrepancy is NOT an efficiency problem — it is the
  low-head tailwater effect. At full 1500 m^3/s the tailwater rises and
  the head collapses below the 8.5 m annual average. Inverting:
      rated head implied at eta = 0.88 : 7.72 m
      rated head implied at eta = 0.85 : 8.00 m
  USE THIS PLANT AS A DELIBERATE NEGATIVE TEST: it proves that pairing an
  AVERAGE head with a DESIGN flow is invalid for low-head schemes, and that
  a tool must either accept a rated head or model H(Q).
  Sources:
    https://www.fichtner.de/en/projects/detailpage/construction-of-rheinfelden-run-of-river-hydropower-plant-germany
    https://www.fwt.fichtner.de/en/projekte/detailseite/new-weir-and-hydropower-plant-at-rheinfelden-germany
    https://www.renewableenergyworld.com/energy-business/new-project-development/swiss-german-utility-brings-new-100-mw-rheinfelden-hydro-on-line/
    https://www.voith.com/corp-en/turbines-generators/modernization/rheinfelden-germanyswitzerland.html

SUMMARY TABLE (assert targets):
  Plant             P[MW]  Q[m3/s]  H[m]   E[GWh]  eta_impl  PF_impl
  Kaligandaki A      144     141    115     842     0.9053    0.6675
  Upper Tamakoshi    456      66    805     2281    0.8749    0.5710
  Rheinfelden        100    1500      8.5    600    0.7995*   0.6849
  (* average head, not rated head — see comment)

  => eta_implied spans 0.80-0.91; PF_implied spans 0.57-0.69.

========================================================================
5. UNIT TRAPS AND EXACT CONVERSION CONSTANTS
========================================================================
All below are EXACT (derived from 1 ft = 0.3048 m exactly and
1 US gal = 3.785411784 L exactly) unless marked.

FLOW
  1 ft^3/s (cfs) = 0.028316846592 m^3/s          EXACT
  1 m^3/s        = 35.3146667215 ft^3/s          (1/0.028316846592)
  TRAP: feeding cfs into an SI formula overstates power by 35.3146667215x
        (+3431%). Feeding m^3/s into an imperial formula understates by
        the same factor (-97.17%). This is the single most destructive bug.
  1 L/s          = 0.001 m^3/s
  1 US gpm       = 6.30901964e-5 m^3/s ; 1 ft^3/s = 448.8312 US gpm
  1 MGD (US)     = 0.0438126364 m^3/s
  1 acre-ft      = 1233.48183754752 m^3          EXACT
  1 acre-ft/day  = 0.0142763 m^3/s               (approx)

HEAD / LENGTH
  1 ft = 0.3048 m                                EXACT
  1 m  = 3.280839895013123 ft
  TRAP: head in feet used as metres overstates power by 3.2808x (+228%).
  TRAP (compounded): cfs + ft together => 35.3147 * 3.2808 = 115.86x error.

POWER
  1 kW  = 1000 W          ; 1 MW = 1e6 W  = 1000 kW ; 1 GW = 1e9 W
  TRAP: rho*g*Q*H*eta in SI returns WATTS. Labelling 4,169,250 as "kW"
        overstates by 1000x. The shortcut form P[kW] = 9.81*Q*H*eta works
        ONLY because 9.81 is being used as kN/m^3, not N/m^3. Never mix
        9810 (N/m^3) with a kW label.
  1 hp (mechanical/imperial) = 745.699871582 W   EXACT by definition
  1 hp (metric, PS)          = 735.49875 W       EXACT (= 75 * 9.80665)

ENERGY
  1 GWh = 1000 MWh = 1e6 kWh = 1e9 Wh
  1 MWh = 1000 kWh
  1 TWh = 1000 GWh
  TRAP: MWh reported as GWh understates by 1000x; the inverse overstates
        by 1000x. In prefeasibility output, a plant of a few MW produces
        TENS of GWh/yr — if your GWh figure is in the thousands for a
        <10 MW plant, you have a 1000x bug.
  TRAP: kW * h gives kWh, but MW * h gives MWh — mixing kW with an
        assumed-MWh label is a silent 1000x.

TIME
  8760 h/yr (365 d) — standard for annual energy
  8766 h/yr (365.25 d, Julian) — +0.0685%
  8784 h/yr (366 d, leap) — +0.2740%
  1 yr = 31,536,000 s (365 d) ; 31,557,600 s (365.25 d)
  ESHA runoff shortcut Qm = (AARD_mm * AREA_km2)/31536 embeds 365 d.

EFFICIENCY
  TRAP: eta entered as 85 instead of 0.85 -> 100x overstatement. Assert
        0 < eta <= 1 and reject values > 1.

HEAD DEFINITION
  TRAP: gross head used where net head is required. Typical penstock/
        headrace loss is 3-10% of gross head; using gross overstates power
        by that same 3-11%. Kaligandaki A: 130 vs 115 m = +13.0% power,
        driving implied eta from 0.9053 down to 0.8008.

========================================================================
6. REALISTIC RANGES, WITH SOURCES
========================================================================

--- OVERALL EFFICIENCY (turbine x gearbox x generator x transformer) ---
Component values, ESHA 2004 "Guide on How to Develop a Small Hydropower
Plant", Table 6.7 "Typical efficiencies of small turbines" (verbatim):
     Kaplan single regulated  0.91
     Kaplan double regulated  0.93
     Francis                  0.94
     Pelton n nozzles         0.90
     Pelton 1 nozzle          0.89
     Turgo                    0.85
   (ESHA notes these are BEST-EFFICIENCY-POINT values, not efficiency at
    design/maximum discharge.)
ESHA Table 6.8 "Typical efficiencies of small generators" (verbatim):
     10 kW 0.910 | 50 kW 0.940 | 100 kW 0.950 | 250 kW 0.955
     500 kW 0.960 | 1000 kW 0.970
ESHA text (verbatim): "The efficiency should be 95 % for a 100 kW machine

corrections:
Five corrections to the premises in the request:

(1) MINIMUM TURBINE FLOW IS NOT "~20-40% OF DESIGN FLOW" IN GENERAL. That
range is right only for Francis and single-regulated Kaplan. ESHA Layman's
Guidebook Table 3.1 gives, as % of design flow: Pelton 10, Turgo 10,
Kaplan 15, semi-Kaplan 15, cross-flow 15, Francis (spiral and open flume)
30, PROPELLER 65. Hard-coding a single 20-40% cut-off will under-predict
energy for Pelton/Kaplan/crossflow schemes by several percent and badly
over-predict for fixed-blade propeller units. Make f_min a per-turbine-type
lookup. Note also an internal inconsistency in ESHA itself worth deciding on
explicitly: Table 3.1 says Francis 30%, while ESHA sec. 6.2.5 says Francis
is acceptable only "from one half of rated discharge" and warns "Below 40%
of the rated discharge, Francis turbines may show instability". Pick 0.40
for Francis if you want the conservative/bankable number, 0.30 if you want
to match ESHA's own energy software.

(2) THE FDC INTEGRATION IS NOT NATURALLY A TRAPEZOID IN THE REFERENCE
METHOD. ESHA's own procedure is a MIDPOINT (rectangle) rule on 5% strips
using Qmedian of each strip, with the final strip width computed rather than
fixed at 0.05. Trapezoid is fine and arguably better, but if you intend to
reproduce or cross-check ESHA/European Atlas numbers, implement both. The
real accuracy issue is not the rule choice — it is (a) failing to include
D=0 and D=1 as nodes, and (b) trapezoiding across the Q_min cut-out, which
is a genuine step discontinuity in P(D) and must have an inserted node with
P evaluated as 0 on the dry side.

(3) "rho FOR FRESH WATER AT ~10 C" IS 999.7026 kg/m^3, NOT 1000. But the
practical answer is that it does not matter and you should not use it. The
difference between (999.7026, 9.80665) and (1000, 9.81) is 0.064% — three
orders of magnitude smaller than the uncertainty in a prefeasibility flow
record. Use rho=1000, g=9.81 (matching ESHA's gamma = 9.81 kN/m^3), document
it, and set cross-convention test tolerances at 0.1% rather than asserting
exact equality against a "physically correct" 10 C value.

(4) "E = P * 8760" IS NOT ANNUAL ENERGY — IT IS THE CEILING. For the worked
example it gives 36.52 GWh/yr, which presumes 10 m^3/s flows every hour of
the year with zero outages. A real ROR plant at PF 0.55-0.65 would deliver
20-24 GWh. If the calculator ever surfaces P*8760 as "annual generation" it
overstates by roughly a factor of 1.5-2. Label it "theoretical maximum".

(5) AN FDC INTEGRATION PRODUCES A GROSS PLANT FACTOR, NOT A CAPACITY FACTOR.
The FDC carries hydrology only — no forced outages, no planned maintenance,
no curtailment, no station-service load. CF_real = PF_fdc x availability
(0.90-0.97 for hydro) x (1 - aux) x (1 - curtailment). Reporting the raw FDC
result as a capacity factor overstates deliverable energy by 3-10%. Assert
CF_reported <= PF_fdc.

Additional data-quality caveats found while sourcing the real plants:

* Kaligandaki A discharge is inconsistent across sources: 141 m^3/s total
  (rated, most sources) vs 44.86 m^3/s listed per unit on nwrmap
  (3 x 44.86 = 134.58 total). The 134.58 figure back-calculates to an
  implied overall efficiency of 0.9485, which is physically implausible
  (it exceeds Francis BEP 0.94 before any generator loss). Use 141 m^3/s.
  This is itself a useful assert: any implied eta > 0.93 means one of the
  three inputs is wrong, not that the plant is exceptional.

* Rheinfelden's published 8.5 m is an AVERAGE head, not a rated head.
  Pairing it with the 1500 m^3/s design discharge yields an implied
  efficiency of 0.7995, which is far below what a modern Kaplan bulb
  achieves. The physical cause is tailwater rise at full discharge in a
  low-head scheme; the rated head consistent with eta = 0.88 is 7.72 m.
  Do not treat 0.7995 as evidence that low-head plants are inefficient —
  treat it as a regression test proving that average head must never be
  multiplied by design flow. For low-head schemes (H < ~15 m) the tool
  should either require an explicit rated head or model H(Q).

* Kaligandaki A also demonstrates the gross/net head trap numerically:
  gross 130 m gives implied eta 0.8008, net 115 m gives 0.9053. Same plant,
  13% power difference, purely from head definition.

* Upper Tamakoshi is the cleanest validation point in the set: 456 MW,
  66 m^3/s, 805 m rated head -> implied eta 0.8749, against a theoretical
  multi-jet Pelton x generator product of 0.90 x 0.97 = 0.873. Agreement to
  0.2%. Anchor the efficiency assertions on this case.

* IRENA's 53.5% hydropower capacity factor is for ALL newly-commissioned
  hydropower (reservoir included), so it is not a clean ROR benchmark. The
  three back-calculated ROR plant factors here (0.571, 0.668, 0.685) are
  the better target band for a ROR tool.
